findings.title: tWR 26 / tRTP 14 break the tWR = 2 x tRTP pairing (harmless direction) and are both very loose for B-die
findings.current: tWR 26 (13.9 ns), tRTP 14 (7.5 ns), tWTRL 12, tWTRS 4. GDM enabled.
findings.suggested: Set them as an even pair. First step: tRTP 8 / tWR 16, with tWTRL 8 optional (= WR/2) and tWTRS 4 unchanged. If stable, try tRTP 6 / tWR 12. Do not use tRTP 7 / tWR 14: GDM rounds odd tRTP up anyway.
findings.rationale:
1) The pairing. JEDEC/Micron DDR4 sets tWR = 2 x tRTP: MR0 encodes WR and RTP as a single pair (WR26<->RTP13, WR28<->RTP14). Here 2 x 14 = 28, but tWR is 26, so the two values do not match. This is the only hard-rule mismatch in the timing set. It cannot cause errors, because the controller's tRTP 14 is longer than the 13 the DRAM would infer from WR 26.
2) Where the values come from. tRTP 14 equals the JEDEC minimum of 7.5 ns exactly (7.5 ns x 1866.7 MHz = 14.0 clocks), so it is an untouched auto value.
3) Typical values. integralfx's presets are safe 20/10, tight 16/8 and extreme 12/6. anta777's rules (quoted in Taraquin's Zen 3 guide) are WTRL = RTP = WR/2 and WTRS 3-4. Taraquin's 2x8 B-die example at 3800 uses WR 14, RTP 7, WTRL 8 (range 6-12) and WTRS 3.
4) GDM. integralfx: GDM forces even tCL, tCWL, tRTP and tWR, so keep them even.
5) Side benefit. Lowering tRTP also lowers the tRAS floor (tRCD + tRTP) from 29 to 23.
6) Limited benefit for tWR. tWR only affects write-to-precharge. On a single-CCD Zen 3 the CCD-to-IOD write path is half-width, so write bandwidth tops out near 50% of theoretical (integralfx). That makes tWR, tWTRL and tRCDWR low-value on this CPU.
findings.expected_impact: Small. tRTP shortens read-to-precharge on page misses: estimated under 0.5 ns in AIDA latency (not measured) and roughly 0% FPS on a 5800X3D. tWR barely matters because writes are capped by the fabric. The main value is a consistent, standard timing set.
findings.risk: Low. B-die rarely errors from tRTP/tWR at these values. Verify with TM5 (anta777 or usmus config) after the change.
sources: https://github.com/integralfx/MemTestHelper/blob/oc-guide/DDR4%20OC%20Guide.md (tWR/tRTP presets, 'tWR is 2*tRTP as per the Micron DDR4 datasheet... JEDEC', GDM forces even tCL/tCWL/tRTP/tWR, single-CCD write bandwidth ~half)
https://www.overclock.net/threads/a-guide-to-ram-overclocking-on-zen-3.1798093/ (Taraquin; read via Wayback 2023 snapshot: anta777 rules 'WTRL=RTP=WR/2', B-die 3800 example WR 14 / RTP 7 / WTRL 8)

findings.title: tRFC 288 (154 ns) is a reasonable B-die value. The real risk is heat: 4 DIMMs at about 1.55 V next to a 3080 Ti
findings.current: tRFC 288 = 154.3 ns at DDR4-3733. FGR is off (normal 1x refresh). tRFC2 486 and tRFC4 299 are unused. tREFI 14553 = 7.8 us (JEDEC normal). Estimated VDIMM about 1.53-1.56 V. 4 DIMMs side by side. No DIMM temperature reading available.
findings.suggested:
1) Do not tighten tRFC further with 4 DIMMs. Keep 288. It is already a multiple of 16, which anta777's rounding guideline asks for.
2) Test warm. Run TM5 (anta777 extreme or usmus x20) while a GPU load (a game or a GPU stress test) heats the case for at least 30-60 min.
3) If errors or rare reboots appear only when warm, raise tRFC by 16 to 304 (162.9 ns), as Taraquin advises.
4) Leave tREFI at default and FGR off.
5) Improve airflow over the DIMMs if you can.
findings.rationale:
1) Range check. integralfx gives B-die (S8B) a typical tRFC of 120-180 ns. Taraquin's 2x8 B-die example at 3800 and 1.45 V uses 272 (range 256-304), i.e. about 143 ns (135-160 ns). At 154 ns this setup sits at the upper-middle of that range, so it is not aggressive.
2) tRFC2/tRFC4. 486 and 299 are exactly the JEDEC 8 Gb defaults of 260 ns and 160 ns (260 x 1.8667 = 485.3 -> 486; 160 x 1.8667 = 298.7 -> 299). So tRFC was set by hand and the 2x/4x values were left on auto. They are only used when FGR is enabled; ZenStates-Core picks the active tRFC from the FGR mode in 0x5012C[18:16], which is 0 here.
3) Temperature. integralfx: 'tRFC timings are very dependent on temperatures'; RAM ideally runs at about 30-40 °C; you can pass a memtest and still crash in games because the CPU and GPU heat the RAM, so stress the GPU during memory tests.
4) B-die thresholds (anecdotal). ComputerBase users report tight-timing B-die becoming unstable from about 40-50 °C, while XMP stays tolerant to 60 °C or more.
5) Why this system is exposed. 4 DIMMs at about 1.55 V, roughly 0.1 V above the kit's 1.45 V XMP rating, dissipate more heat. The inner DIMMs have no airflow gap, and an RTX 3080 Ti sits directly below.
findings.expected_impact: Stability. This is the most likely cause of warm-only crashes or WHEA-free silent errors in long gaming sessions. Raising tRFC by 16 costs well under 0.5% bandwidth and is not measurable in games on a 5800X3D.
findings.risk: Keeping 288 without a warm test risks rare crashes in summer or long sessions. Going lower (272 or below) raises that risk with 4 DIMMs.
sources: https://github.com/integralfx/MemTestHelper/blob/oc-guide/DDR4%20OC%20Guide.md (S8B tRFC 120-180 ns; 'Temperatures and Its Effect on Stability')

https://www.overclock.net/threads/a-guide-to-ram-overclocking-on-zen-3.1798093/ (Taraquin via Wayback: B-die RFC 272 (256-304) at 3800; 'If you get rare bluescreens and reboots try raising RFC by 16')

findings.title: tRDRDSCL / tWRWRSCL 5/5 are at the 'hurts bandwidth' edge. B-die normally runs 4/4 or lower
findings.current: tRDRDSCL 5, tWRWRSCL 5. tRDRDSC 1 and tWRWRSC 1 are already at the minimum.
findings.suggested:
1) Set 4/4 and run TM5.
2) Then try 3/3.
3) If only one of them fails, tRDRDSCL is usually the one that needs +1, e.g. 4/3.
4) Prioritise tRDRDSCL. Write bandwidth on a single-CCD 5800X3D is capped by the fabric anyway.
findings.rationale:
1) What SCL is. SCL is the extra spacing between back-to-back CAS commands to the same bank group. anta777: SC = tCCD_S - 3 = 1 and SCL = tCCD_L - 3 = 2, 3 or 4. SCL 5 therefore means tCCD_L = 8 clocks.
2) Guide values. integralfx: Safe 4/4, Tight 3/3, Extreme 2/2; 'values above 5 greatly hurt bandwidth'; 2 is 'extremely difficult for all but... B-Die'; 'tRDRDSCL will be the one that needs to be run 1 or even 2 values higher'. Taraquin's baseline for every good die is RDRDSCL 4 / WRWRSCL 4.
3) Assessment. 5/5 looks like an AGESA auto value. Among the remaining knobs it is the one with the clearest bandwidth effect.
findings.expected_impact: A few percent higher read bandwidth in AIDA-type tests is typical (estimate, not measured here). In games on a 5800X3D it is probably under 1% average FPS. PCGH measured the whole DDR4-3200 CL16 -> 3800 tuned step at only +1.9 to +3.5% on the X3D, versus up to +7.2% on the 5800X, because the 96 MB L3 hides memory.
findings.risk: Low to moderate. With 4 DIMMs on a daisy-chain board and unknown ProcODT/RTT, 3/3 may not be stable. Errors show up quickly in TM5. Change one value at a time.
sources: https://www.overclock.net/threads/a-guide-to-ram-overclocking-on-zen-3.1798093/ (Taraquin via Wayback: RDRDSCL 4 / WRWRSCL 4; anta777 'SC=CCDS-3=1, SCL=CCDL-3=2,3,4')

findings.title: With 4x single-rank, only the DD (different-DIMM) turnarounds matter; SD is unused. tRDRDDD 6 / tWRWRDD 7 are loose
findings.current: tRDRDSD 4, tRDRDDD 6, tWRWRSD 6, tWRWRDD 7. Chip selects: CS0 on (0x50000=0x1), CS1 off, CS2 on (0x50008=0x201), CS3 off on both UMCs, i.e. one rank per DIMM and two DIMMs per channel.
findings.suggested:
1) Ignore the SD values; you may set them equal to DD for tidiness.
2) Lower tRDRDDD from 6 to 5 and test. Then try 4.
3) Lower tWRWRDD from 7 to 6.
4) Start at 5 rather than 4 because the DQS-preamble mode is ambiguous (see rationale).
findings.rationale:
1) Naming. AMD/ZenTimings names: SC = same chip select, SD = same DIMM but a different rank, DD = different DIMM. CoreFreq names the fields tscRdTRd, tsdRdTRd and tddRdTRd (0x50220 [19:16]/[11:8]/[3:0]) and the matching WrTWr fields at 0x50224.
2) Why SD is unused. Each DIMM has a single rank (CS1 and CS3 are disabled), so a same-DIMM/different-rank switch never happens. Every rank switch is a DIMM switch, and it happens often because the controller interleaves between the two ranks in each channel.
3) Guides. integralfx: 'dr only affects dual rank sticks... dd only needs to be considered when you run two DIMMs per channel'; 'tRDRD_dr/dd can be lowered... to 5 for a large bump in read bandwidth' (written for Intel; the concept is the same). anta777 (in Taraquin's guide): SD = DD, RDRDSD/DD = 4 + RPRE - 1, WRWRSD/DD = 4 + WPRE - 1. That gives 4 with 1T preambles and 5 with 2T preambles.
4) Preamble ambiguity. The snapshot has Preamble2t = 1 at 0x50200[12] (CoreFreq comment: '1: 2T DQS preambles enabled'), yet RDPRE/WRPRE at 0x502A4 decode to 1. The floor may therefore be 5. Unverified.
findings.expected_impact: Read bandwidth improves on this 2DPC setup (estimated low single-digit %, not measured). Game impact on the X3D is likely under 1%. tWRWRDD gains are mostly hidden by the write-bandwidth cap.
findings.risk: Moderate. DD gaps cover the bus and ODT handover between the two DIMMs on a daisy-chain board. If set too low you get read/write errors, possibly only when warm. Test each step.
sources: CoreFreq x86_64/amd_reg.h @20de51c, AMD_17_UMC_TIMING_DTR8/9/10 (field names tddRdTRd/tsdRdTRd/tscRdTRd; Preamble2T comment line 1999): https://github.com/cyring/CoreFreq/blob/master/x86_64/amd_reg.h
https://www.overclock.net/threads/a-guide-to-ram-overclocking-on-zen-3.1798093/ (Taraquin via Wayback: anta777 SD=DD, RDRDSD/DD=4+RPRE-1, WRWRSD/DD=4+WPRE-1)

findings.title: tRAS 36 / tRC 51 are consistent (tRC = tRAS + tRP exactly) but about 6 clocks looser than typical B-die
findings.current: tRAS 36 (19.3 ns), tRC 51 (27.3 ns), tRP 15, tRCDRD 15, tRTP 14. tRAS floor = tRCD + tRTP = 29, so the rule is met.
findings.suggested: Set tRAS 30 and tRC 45 (= 30 + 15). After tRTP is reduced to 8, the floor is 23, but do not go below tRAS about 28 / tRC about 43. Keep tRC = tRAS + tRP.
findings.rationale:
1) Rules. integralfx: 'Set tRAS = tRCD(RD) + tRTP... This is the absolute minimum'; 'Set tRC = tRP + tRAS'. integralfx's own test showed low tRC causing instant errors even when tRAS was fine. Taraquin: RAS = CL + RCD (= 29 here), RC = RAS + RP. anta777: RAS = RC - RP.
2) Typical B-die. Taraquin's 2x8 B-die example at 3800 uses RAS 30 (range 21-32) and RC 45 (range 30-50).
3) Result. tRC 45 at 3733 is 24.1 ns.
findings.expected_impact: Small: slightly faster bank-conflict row cycling, a fraction of a ns of latency. Roughly 0-0.5% in games on the X3D (estimate).
findings.risk: Low to moderate. tRC that is too low produces errors quickly. Raise tRC first if errors appear.
sources: https://www.overclock.net/threads/a-guide-to-ram-overclocking-on-zen-3.1798093/ (Taraquin via Wayback: RAS=CL+RCD, RC=RAS+RP; B-die example RAS 30 RC 45)

findings.title: tRDWR 10 / tWRRD 3 / tCWL 14 suit two ranks per channel. Keep tWRRD at 3; tRDWR 9 is optional
findings.current: tRDWR 10, tWRRD 3, tCWL 14 (= tCL 14, even).
findings.suggested:
1) Keep tWRRD at 3. Do not copy the single-rank 1-DIMM-per-channel value of 1.
2) Optionally try tRDWR 9.
3) Keep tCWL = tCL = 14. tCWL 12 would need a higher tWRRD and only speeds up writes, which the fabric caps.
findings.rationale:
1) tWRRD. Taraquin: 'WRRD 1 on SR, 3 on DR'. CoreFreq names the field at 0x50228[3:0] tddWrTRd, i.e. write-to-read to another rank or DIMM. Same-rank write-to-read is governed by tWTRS/L. With 4x SR there are two ranks per channel, which makes the bus behave like dual rank, so 3 is the right value.
2) tRDWR. Taraquin's 2x8 B-die example is 8 (range 7-10), with +1 or +2 for dual rank, giving 9-10 here. anta777's theoretical floor, CL - CWL + 5 + WPRE, is 6 (or 7 with 2T WPRE).
3) tCWL. integralfx: 'On AMD, tCWL can often be set to tCL - 2 but is known to require higher tWRRD'. Taraquin's baseline is CWL = CL, and anta777's is CL = CWL even.
findings.expected_impact: Negligible. tRDWR 9 might add a little mixed read/write throughput.
findings.risk: Low for tRDWR 9. Setting tWRRD to 1 or 2 with 2DPC risks errors.
sources: https://www.overclock.net/threads/a-guide-to-ram-overclocking-on-zen-3.1798093/ (Taraquin via Wayback: RDWR 8 (7-10), WRRD 1 SR / 3 DR, CWL=CL)

findings.title: GDM rounding costs nothing here: tCL, tCWL, tWR and tRTP are already even, and the odd tRCD/tRP are not rounded
findings.current: GDM Enabled, Cmd 1T. tCL 14, tCWL 14, tWR 26, tRTP 14 (all even). tRCDRD/tRCDWR 15 and tRP 15 (odd).
findings.suggested: No change. When tuning, keep tCL, tCWL, tWR and tRTP even. Do not attempt GDM off at 1T with 4 DIMMs unless you are ready to tune CAD drive strengths and setup times, which currently cannot be read.
findings.rationale:
1) Rounding. integralfx: GDM forces even tCL, tCWL, tRTP and tWR (e.g. CL15 becomes 16). tRCD and tRP are not affected, so tRCD/tRP 15 really run at 15.
2) Performance order (integralfx). GDM off at 1T is fastest, then GDM on at 1T, then GDM off at 2T. The current GDM on / 1T is the best practical option with 2 DIMMs per channel.
3) Testing note. Taraquin notes that GDM can mask instabilities, which favours long TM5 runs.
findings.expected_impact: None.
findings.risk: None as-is.

findings.title: tRRDS/tRRDL/tFAW 4/4/16 are already at the floor and consistent (tFAW = 4 x tRRDS)
findings.current: tRRDS 4, tRRDL 4, tFAW 16.
findings.suggested: Keep. If instability appears after the BIOS update, the first cheap fallback is tRRDL 6 (Taraquin's B-die example), which costs almost no performance.
findings.rationale:
1) tFAW. integralfx: 'The minimum value for which lowering tFAW will affect the performance of RAM is tRRDS * 4'. 16 = 4 x 4, so tFAW is not a limiting factor.
2) How aggressive this is. 4/4/16 is integralfx's 'Extreme' preset. Taraquin's B-die 3800 example uses RRDS 4, RRDL 6, FAW 16.
findings.expected_impact: None (already optimal).
findings.risk: Slightly aggressive with 4 DIMMs, but presumably proven stable on the current BIOS.

findings.title: tMOD/tMRD/PDA, tSTAG, tCKE and tREFI are auto or JEDEC values with no runtime performance relevance
findings.current: tMOD 28, tMODPDA 28, tMRD 8, tMRDPDA 19, tSTAG 218 (116.8 ns), tCKE 1, PowerDown Disabled, tREFI 14553 (7.79 us).
findings.suggested: No change.
findings.rationale:
1) Mode-register timings. tMOD 28 = 15 ns and tMRDPDA 19 = 10 ns (18.67 rounded up), with tMRD 8 nCK. These match JEDEC DDR4 formulas as I recall them: tMOD = max(24nCK, 15 ns), tMRD = 8 nCK, tMRD_PDA = max(16nCK, 10 ns), tMOD_PDA = tMOD. I did not re-check them against the JESD79-4 text. They only apply around mode-register writes during training and init.
2) tSTAG. CoreFreq calls it 'Min Delay between REF cmd', i.e. the refresh stagger between ranks. It only matters for refresh scheduling across the two DIMMs and is AGESA-controlled. A Gigabyte menu item for it is unverified.
3) tCKE. 1 is below JEDEC's max(3nCK, 5 ns), which is about 10 clocks here. It is inert because PowerDown is disabled; integralfx: disabling PowerDown 'eliminates the need to tune related timings such as tCKE and tXP'.
4) tREFI. 7.8 us is the JEDEC normal-temperature interval and the right choice for warm B-die (integralfx warns that raised tREFI breaks with seasonal temperature changes).
findings.expected_impact: None.
findings.risk: None.
sources: CoreFreq amd_reg.h AMD_17_UMC_TIMING_DTR13 and tSTAG comment (line 2242)

findings.title: After flashing F19c, re-enter every manual timing and re-snapshot: check tPHYRDL symmetry and any changed auto values
findings.current: Both UMCs are register-identical, including tPHYRDL 26/26, tPHYWRL 9 and RDDATAEN 9. tRFC was hand-set (tRFC2/4 are JEDEC auto). Several tertiaries look like auto values (SCL 5/5, DD 6/7, tRTP 14).
findings.suggested:
1) Before flashing, write down or photograph every manual value (tCL through tRFC, tRRDL 4, tFAW 16, tWTRL 12, tRDWR 10, tWRRD 3), plus VDIMM and VSOC.
2) After the flash and CMOS reset, re-enter them explicitly. Do not rely on the new AGESA's auto tables.
3) Re-run the snapshot and diff it against 20261024-181828_F16b.
4) Confirm tPHYRDL is still equal on both channels over 3-5 cold boots.
5) Then apply the tightening steps above one at a time with TM5.
findings.rationale:
1) Auto values move. A new AGESA (1.2.0.8 -> 1.2.0.12) can change auto-derived tertiaries and training results. Matching channels are the current baseline.
2) tPHYRDL mismatches. Forum reports of 26/28 tPHYRDL mismatches tie them to training differences between channels; whether a mismatch is harmful is unresolved (from search results; the forum posts themselves were not readable).
3) Diffing. The ZenStates-Core register decode already in use makes the before/after comparison exact.
findings.expected_impact: Avoids silently losing the tuned tRFC/tRRD settings or picking up looser auto tertiaries after the update.
findings.risk: None.
sources: snapshot.json (UMC0 and UMC1 raw registers identical)

review.notes:
Method: I decoded every timing from the raw UMC registers in snapshot.json (both channels match) and checked it against hard constraints and rules of thumb. Sources: integralfx's DDR4 OC guide (fetched raw from GitHub); Taraquin's OCN Zen 3 guide, which includes anta777's formulas (read from a 2023 Wayback snapshot because OCN is paywalled for bots); CoreFreq amd_reg.h field names; and PCGH's 5800X3D RAM-scaling test.

Hard checks that pass:
- tRC 51 = tRAS 36 + tRP 15
- tRAS 36 >= tRCD + tRTP = 29
- tFAW 16 = 4 x tRRDS
- tRRDL >= tRRDS, tWTRL >= tWTRS
- tCWL = tCL, both even
- All GDM-rounded timings (tCL, tCWL, tWR, tRTP) are even
- tRDWR 10 is above anta777's floor of 6-7
- tPHYRDL matches across channels
- tREFI is the JEDEC 7.8 us
- tMOD 28 and tMRDPDA 19 equal 15 ns and 10 ns exactly

The only hard-rule mismatch is tWR 26 vs 2 x tRTP = 28. It is harmless in that direction.

Evidence on the configuration:
- tRFC2 486 and tRFC4 299 equal the JEDEC 8 Gb defaults of 260 ns and 160 ns exactly. So tRFC 288 was set by hand and the 2x/4x values are unused (FGR = 0).
- CS0 and CS2 are enabled and CS1 and CS3 are disabled. That proves one rank per DIMM, so only the DD turnarounds matter; SD is never used.

Tuning priority on a 5800X3D:
- Order: tRDRDSCL first, then tRDRDDD, then tRAS/tRC/tRTP. tRFC: hold.
- Expect small gains. PCGH measured only +1.9 to +3.5% for the X3D from DDR4-3200 CL16 to DDR4-3800 tuned, against up to +7.2% on the 5800X.
- Write-side timings pay off least because single-CCD write bandwidth is capped at about half of theoretical. These are tRCDWR 15 (anta777 suggests 8), tWRWRSCL, tWRWRDD, tWR and tCWL. I did not list tRCDWR as a separate finding for that reason.

Open or unverified:
- The 2T-preamble state. Preamble2t = 1 per CoreFreq's comment, but RDPRE/WRPRE decode to 1. This affects whether the DD floor is 4 or 5.
- The JEDEC formulas for tMOD, tMRD and the PDA variants are from memory. The JESD79-4 and Micron/Samsung PDFs could not be downloaded.
- B-die temperature thresholds are forum anecdotes (40-50 °C for tight timings).
- The TechPowerUp and tPHYRDL forum posts returned 403, so the tPHYRDL claims rely on search snippets.

Out of this lens, not assessed: BGS Disabled with BGS Alt Enabled; ProcODT, RTT and CAD settings (unreadable); FCLK and voltages.

Local copies:
- /tmp/rules_dl/ddr4oc.md (integralfx guide)
- /tmp/rules_dl/taraquin.txt (extracted first post of the guide)

verdicts.reason: The arithmetic checks out: 2x14=28, not 26; 7.5 ns x 1.8667 = 14.0 clk; the tRAS floor drops from 29 to 23. The integralfx quotes match /tmp/rules_dl/ddr4oc.md lines 566-572 and 394. Three things are overstated. (1) 'Only hard-rule mismatch': the MR0 WR/RTP pair only sets the DRAM's internal auto-precharge (RDA/WRA) timing. The UMC's tRTP and tWR registers are separate. Other values also break JEDEC: tWR 26 = 13.9 ns, below JEDEC 15 ns (= 28 clk), so tWR 26 is not a JEDEC auto value (manual or an AGESA clamp, unverified); tCKE 1 is below max(3nCK, 5 ns) = 10 clk. (2) Benefit of tRTP alone: tRAS 36 > tRCD+tRTP 29, so tRTP only limits precharge for reads issued more than 22 clk after ACT. Lowering tRTP without lowering tRAS gains almost nothing, so the two belong together. (3) The integralfx extreme 12/6 step buys nothing measurable on an X3D with 4 DIMMs. The GDM note is consistent: tRTP 7 would effectively be 8.
verdicts.corrected_suggested: If you tune at all, set tWR 16 / tRTP 8 (tWTRL 8 optional) in the same session as the tRAS/tRC reduction, then run a warm memory test. Skip the 12/6 step. Treat the WR/RTP mismatch as cosmetic, not a rule violation.
verdicts.corrected_impact: No measurable gaming change on the 5800X3D. At most a sub-ns reduction in page-miss latency, and only when tRAS is lowered too.

verdicts.reason: The numbers are verified: 288 clk = 154.3 ns; 486 and 299 are exactly the JEDEC 8 Gb 260 ns and 160 ns values (ceil of 485.3 and 298.7); 304 clk = 162.9 ns. Refresh overhead is 288/14553 = 1.98% vs 304/14553 = 2.09% (delta 0.11%), so 'well under 0.5%' holds. The integralfx temperature quotes (ddr4oc.md lines 304-309) and Taraquin's 'raise RFC by 16' (taraquin.txt) are verified. Corrections: (a) TM5 is a Windows tool and the user runs Bazzite Linux, so the test plan needs Linux tools. (b) The anta777 rounding rule, as quoted by Taraquin, is 'divisible by 8 on 8gb sticks, by 16 on 16gb sticks... apparently only applies to Intel and Micron', so the multiple-of-16 point is irrelevant here. (c) 'Most likely cause of warm-only crashes' is speculative: no crash or error has been reported. (d) The heat risk is understated on voltage. Estimated VDIMM 1.53-1.56 V is at integralfx's S8B daily ceiling ('Up to 1.55'; above that is 'Extreme... A RAM fan is recommended', ddr4oc.md ~line 283) and above the JEDEC absolute maximum of 1.50 V that integralfx quotes. (e) DIMM temperature cannot be read: the FCH SMBus 00:14.0 [1022:790b] has no driver bound even though i2c_piix4 is loaded, so jc42/ee1004 are unavailable. A warm test is the only check. (f) 'RTX 3080 Ti directly below' the DIMMs is imprecise: the GPU sits below the socket. A flow-through (FE-style) cooler exhausting upward would still matter.
verdicts.corrected_suggested: Keep tRFC 288 with FGR off and default tREFI. Confirm the real VDIMM in BIOS PC Health ('DRAM Channel A/B Voltage') before deciding anything. Test warm on Linux for 1-2 h with a game or GPU stress load running at the same time: stressapptest (e.g. -M <~85% of free RAM> -s 3600 -W) or memtester, run from a toolbox/distrobox or layered package, plus a bootable memtest86+ pass. If errors appear only when warm, go to 304 (+16) and/or improve DIMM airflow.
verdicts.corrected_impact: Stability only. tRFC 288 to 304 costs about 0.1% of DRAM time, which is unmeasurable in games. The warm test matters more than the tRFC value.

verdicts.reason: integralfx says 'values such as 5 are acceptable... Values above 5 greatly hurt bandwidth' (ddr4oc.md line 619). So 5/5 is explicitly acceptable, not at the 'hurts bandwidth' edge, and the title overstates it. The 4/4 baseline is right (Taraquin) and so are the anta777 formulas. Missed interaction: GDM latches commands at half the DRAM clock (AMD, via Guru3D), and FuturePlus says 'All timing parameters are rounded up to an even number of clock cycles.' If anta777's SCL = tCCD_L - 3 offset is right, SCL 4 gives tCCD_L 7 (odd), which effectively becomes 8, the same as SCL 5. The next effective step would then be SCL 3. The offset is unverified, so 5 to 4 may change nothing. The 'a few percent' read-bandwidth claim is unmeasured. With BankGroupEn and BGS Alt on, same-bank-group back-to-back CAS is a minority of streaming traffic, so expect about 1-2% at most. PCGH's +1.9 to +3.5% for the X3D was for the whole 3200 CL16 to 3800 16-15-15 step, which I verified.
verdicts.corrected_suggested: Optional. Try 4/4 and measure read bandwidth before and after on Linux (e.g. lmbench bw_mem or STREAM). If nothing changes (as GDM parity would predict), try 3/3, or 4/3 with tRDRDSCL higher. Otherwise leave 5/5, which integralfx calls acceptable. Change one value at a time and test warm.
verdicts.corrected_impact: About 0-2% synthetic read bandwidth, possibly zero for SCL 4 under GDM. Roughly 0% FPS on the 5800X3D.

verdicts.reason: The core claim holds and I found stronger evidence for it. CS1 and CS3 are disabled (0x50004 = 0x5000C = 0), so SD is never used. The chip-select masks 0x50020 and 0x50024 are both 0x3FFFDFE, which has exactly one zero bit (bit 9), and CS2's base 0x201 sets that bit. By Linux amd64_edac calculate_cs_size(), that means each CS is 8 GB and CS0/CS2 are two-way interleaved. DIMM-to-DIMM switches are therefore constant and DD matters. Corrections: (1) The 'preamble ambiguity' largely resolves. 0x502A4 WRPRE/RDPRE rows appear only on ZenTimings' DDR5/LPDDR5 panels (WPF/Controls/*DDR5*.xaml) and the register reads 0x00000000 on both UMCs here. RDPRE/WRPRE = 1 is therefore a decode artifact. Preamble2t = 1 (0x50200 bit 12, CoreFreq: '1: 2T DQS preambles enabled') is the DDR4-relevant bit, so the anta777 floor is 5, not 4. (2) anta777's formulas are not reliable floors in AMD register units: the same set gives WRRD = CWL-CL+4+RPRE = 5-6, yet tWRRD 3 is running. (3) integralfx's 'lower to 5' is in Intel register units and does not transfer numerically. (4) GDM parity may make odd steps no-ops.
verdicts.corrected_suggested: Ignore SD. Try tRDRDDD 6 to 5 and tWRWRDD 7 to 6 to 5, one at a time, and measure read and mixed bandwidth. Stop at 5; do not try 4 while 2T preamble is active. Test warm, because DD margins cover ODT handover on a 2DPC daisy-chain with unknown RTT.
verdicts.corrected_impact: Small synthetic bandwidth gain in 2DPC mixed-DIMM traffic (unmeasured, likely 1-3%). About 0-1% in games on the X3D.

verdicts.reason: Verified: 36 clk = 19.3 ns, 51 clk = 27.3 ns, 51 = 36 + 15, floor 15 + 14 = 29, tRC 45 = 24.1 ns. The quotes match integralfx steps 7-8 (lines 645-660) and Taraquin (RAS = CL + RCD, RC = RAS + RP; B-die example RAS 30 (21-32), RC 45 (30-50)). tRAS and tRC are bank-internal and do not depend on DIMM count. One nuance: under GDM, command spacing is effectively even, so tRC 45 behaves like 46 (24.6 ns). The current 51 already behaves like 52. Entering tRC 46 is equivalent and avoids false precision. The 28/43 floor is an arbitrary safety margin, not a rule, which is fine.

Keeping tWRRD 3 (Taraquin: 'WRRD 1 on SR, 3 on DR'; two ranks per channel here) and tCWL = tCL = 14 is sound. Corrections: (1) Under GDM, half-rate command latching makes command-to-command spacing even, so tRDWR 9 most likely behaves like 10 (if the register is in plain clocks, which is unverified). The next real step, 8, is below Taraquin's dual-rank-adjusted 9-10, so the 'optional tRDWR 9' is probably a no-op. (2) The tCWL rationale conflicts with anta777's own formulas. RDWR = CL-CWL+5+WPRE and WRRD = CWL-CL+4+RPRE mean a lower tCWL raises the read-to-write requirement and lowers write-to-read, the opposite of the integralfx line quoted. The conclusion (keep CWL = CL) does not change. (3) CoreFreq also names the tRDWR field 'tddRdTWr' (DTR10 [12:8]), so its 'dd' prefix does not decide the tWRRD semantics. The cross-rank reading is plausible but unverified.
verdicts.corrected_suggested: Keep tWRRD 3, tRDWR 10 and tCWL = tCL = 14. Skip tRDWR 9, since GDM likely makes it equal to 10. Only test tRDWR 8 if bandwidth is measured and errors are checked warm.
verdicts.corrected_impact: None expected.

verdicts.reason: The central claim, that odd tRCD/tRP are not rounded and 'really run at 15', is very likely wrong. AMD's own memory blog (summarised by Guru3D) says 'GDM allows the RAM to use a clock that's one half the true DRAM frequency for the purposes of latching' the command/address bus. FuturePlus, a DDR protocol-analyzer vendor, says that in gear-down mode 'All timing parameters are rounded up to an even number of clock cycles.' Commands can only land on every other clock, so ACT-to-RD (tRCD), PRE-to-ACT (tRP) and ACT-to-ACT (tRC) spacing is effectively even. tRCDRD/tRCDWR 15, tRP 15 and tRC 51 therefore act as 16/16/52, and 'GDM costs nothing here' is false: about 1 clk (0.54 ns) each. integralfx's list (tCL, tCWL, tRTP, tWR) is what the BIOS rounds in mode-register settings, not the whole effect. The recommendation to keep GDM on at 1T with 4 DIMMs, and not to attempt GDM-off without CAD/ODT data, stands.
verdicts.corrected_suggested: Keep GDM on at 1T. Treat odd primaries as their next even value and tune in even steps: tRCD/tRP 15 = 16 effectively, so the next real step is 14 (within Taraquin's B-die range of 14-17). Only test it warm, if at all. Re-check odd settings elsewhere in the same way (tRC 51/45, tRDWR 9, possibly SCL/DD depending on register offset).
verdicts.corrected_impact: GDM currently costs about 0.5 ns each on tRCD, tRP and tRC. A real tRCD/tRP 14 would save about 1 ns of page-miss latency, about 0% FPS on the X3D.

verdicts.reason: 16 = 4 x 4. integralfx line 569: 'The minimum value for which lowering tFAW will affect the performance of RAM is tRRDS * 4 or tRRDL * 4, whichever is lower.' 4/4/16 is integralfx's Extreme preset (line 565). Taraquin's B-die example uses 4/6/16. All values are even, so GDM parity has no effect. Using tRRDL 6 as the first fallback is cheap and sensible.

Arithmetic checks out: tMOD 28 = 15 ns x 1.8667; tMRDPDA 19 = ceil(18.67); tSTAG 218 = 116.8 ns; tREFI 14553 / 1866.67 MHz = 7.80 us. The decodes match the raw registers (0x50234 = 0x1C131C08, 0x50250 = 0xDA0000, 0x50254 = 0x0104000C). The JEDEC formulas quoted match my own knowledge of JESD79-4 but were not re-checked against the PDF (the local 'PDFs' in /tmp/rules_dl are HTML error pages). Small notes: integralfx (line 140) says tREFI 'isn't modifiable on AMD', so 'leave tREFI' is moot on most Zen 3 boards. tCKE also governs self-refresh entry and exit, but it is inert in normal operation with PowerDown disabled.

The direction is right: re-enter manual values, re-snapshot and diff, check that tPHYRDL matches across boots. But it leaves out the settings most likely to matter for 2DPC stability after a flash, which Linux cannot read: ProcODT, RttNom/Wr/Park, CAD bus drive strengths and setup times, VDDG CCD/IOD, VDDP, and the VDIMM set value. These go back to auto when Gigabyte's required 'Load Optimized Defaults' runs (manual p.38, per research/bios.md). Saved profiles are reported not to carry across BIOS versions. The snapshot tool already says a one-time 'rpm-ostree kargs --append=iomem=relaxed' boot makes the AOD/APOB tables readable, which would capture these values exactly. research/bios.md also notes that F16b is no longer downloadable (404), so a Q-Flash 'Save BIOS' backup is the only rollback. And pm_table 0x380905 offsets may change with the new SMU firmware, so the snapshot's voltage and clock readout must be re-validated. The tPHYRDL claims rest on search snippets (unverified).
verdicts.corrected_suggested: Before flashing: (1) photograph every BIOS page for DRAM timings, voltages (VDIMM, VSOC, VDDG CCD/IOD, VDDP), ProcODT/RTT and CAD settings, or boot once with iomem=relaxed and re-run the snapshot to capture AOD/APOB; (2) Q-Flash 'Save BIOS to Drive' to back up F16b. After the flash: load Optimized Defaults, re-enter all values explicitly including ODT/RTT/CAD and voltages, re-snapshot, diff, check pm_table version and offsets, and check tPHYRDL over several cold boots. Then run a warm stability test before any tightening.
verdicts.corrected_impact: Avoids silently losing the trained/tuned state, including the ODT/RTT/CAD values that a 4-DIMM daisy-chain setup depends on.

missed: GDM rounding affects the whole tuning plan. AMD: 'GDM allows the RAM to use a clock that's one half the true DRAM frequency for the purposes of latching' (https://www.guru3d.com/story/amd-blogs-on-ryzen-memory-performance/). FuturePlus: 'All timing parameters are rounded up to an even number of clock cycles' (https://futureplus.com/what-is-ddr4-memory-gear-down-mode). The reviewer keeps GDM on but plans 1-clock steps throughout. The current odd tRCD 15, tRP 15 and tRC 51 already act as 16/16/52. Suggested odd steps (tRC 45, tRDWR 9, and possibly SCL 4 or DD 5, depending on the unverified register offsets) may do nothing. Use even effective targets and measure bandwidth or latency before and after.

The test and error-monitoring advice is Windows-centric for a Bazzite Linux user. TM5 is a Windows program, and none of stressapptest, memtester, memtest86+, y-cruncher or rasdaemon is installed (checked with command -v). On Linux, use stressapptest or memtester from a toolbox/distrobox or layered package, plus a bootable memtest86+, with a concurrent GPU load. For fabric/FCLK errors (the WHEA-19 equivalent), watch 'journalctl -k' for 'mce: [Hardware Error]' entries. The current kernel journal has none, but it only covers about 4 h of a roughly 42 h uptime (single boot entry starting at monotonic 150500 s).

Before the flash, capture the BIOS-only memory parameters. AOD/APOB failed only because of the EPERM on /dev/mem (snapshot.md lines 60-70). One boot with 'rpm-ostree kargs --append=iomem=relaxed' would record ProcODT, RTT and CAD drive strengths, which matter most for 4 DIMMs on a daisy-chain board and will reset to auto with Optimized Defaults after F19c. Also back up F16b with Q-Flash 'Save BIOS': research/bios.md says F16b now returns 404 on Gigabyte's server.

VDIMM is at or above the B-die daily ceiling, and no rules finding addresses it directly. The estimated 1.53-1.56 V (IT8792E in1 DDRVTT 0.763 V x2, scaled against the PR #1036 reference board) sits at integralfx's S8B 'Daily Voltage: Up to 1.55' limit; above that is 'Extreme... A RAM fan is recommended' (ddr4oc.md around line 283). It is also above the JEDEC JESD79-4B absolute maximum of 1.50 V that integralfx quotes. Confirm it in BIOS PC Health ('DRAM Channel A/B Voltage') before flashing. Since 4 DIMMs at this voltage sit next to the GPU's heat, this matters more than any tertiary timing.

DIMM temperature and SPD cannot be read on this system right now. The FCH SMBus controller 00:14.0 [1022:790b] has no driver bound (no /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:00:14.0/driver) even though i2c_piix4 is loaded, and /sys/bus/i2c/devices only lists NVIDIA adapters. So ee1004 (SPD, which would settle the two-kit/XMP question) and jc42 (a thermal sensor, if the modules even have one; the Thaiphoon screenshot shows none) are unavailable. The temperature-sensitive tRFC advice therefore depends entirely on warm testing.

The cost-benefit framing is missing. PCGH measured the entire DDR4-3200 16-18-18 to DDR4-3800 16-15-15 step at only +1.9/+2.6/+3.5% in games on the 5800X3D, versus +2.3/+6.1/+7.2% on the 5800X (verified, https://www.pcgameshardware.de/Ryzen-7-5800X3D-CPU-278064/Specials/Ryzen-7-5800X3D-5800X-RAM-Skalierung-3D-V-Cache-1394526/2/). The proposed tertiary and secondary tweaks together are very likely under 1% FPS. With 4 DIMMs at about 1.55 V and silent-corruption risk, the highest-value actions are verifying stability, capturing settings before the flash, and restoring them faithfully afterwards, not further tightening.

The preamble decode artifact matters for the DD floor. ZenTimings shows RDPRE/WRPRE (0x502A4) only on DDR5/LPDDR5 panels (/tmp/verify_src/ZenTimings/WPF/Controls/*DDR5*.xaml), and the register is 0x00000000 on both UMCs. Preamble2t = 1 at 0x50200 bit 12 is the meaningful DDR4 field, which points to 2T preambles and a DD floor of 5, not 4.

findings.title: Actual VDIMM is about 1.53-1.56 V, at the top of the B-die daily range, with 4 tightly packed DIMMs above a 3080 Ti
findings.current: IT8792E in1 'DDRVTT AB' reads 0.763 V (ADC count 70; 10 samples in a row all 763 mV). DDR4 VTT = VDDQ/2, and the reference B550 AORUS PRO showed 0.682 V VTT at 1.380 V DRAM (ratio 2.02), so VDIMM is about 1.53-1.56 V (+/-30 mV). The XMP rating is 1.45 V (4400 19-19-19). Settings: DDR4-3733 CL14-15-15, tRFC 288 = 154 ns, 2 DIMMs per channel. DMI's '1.2 V' is only the SPD nominal value.
findings.suggested: 1) Read the real value in BIOS Settings > PC Health 'DRAM Channel A/B Voltage' (field name from the Gigabyte manual p.32). 2) Treat about 1.55 V as read there as the daily ceiling for these 4 DIMMs. Never run above 1.60 V daily, because of the Ryzen 5000 DDR PHY. If it reads above 1.56 V, lower 'DRAM Voltage (CH A/B)' 10-20 mV at a time and retest. If errors only appear when the RAM is warm, loosen tRFC (e.g. 288 -> 304-312, about 163-167 ns) rather than adding voltage. 3) Make sure there is front-to-back airflow across the DIMM slots; a small fan over the DIMMs is cheap insurance. 4) Heat-soak test: run a memory test at the same time as a GPU load for at least 1 h. 5) Do not read IT8792E in5 ('PM_CLDO12', about 1.50 V) as VDIMM.
findings.rationale: Several sources put this voltage at the edge of daily use. integralfx DDR4 OC guide: S8B 'Daily: up to 1.55 V, Extreme: above 1.55 V (RAM fan recommended)'. The same guide says 'daily use of VDIMM voltages above 1.60 V on Ryzen 3000 and 5000 ... is not advisable' because of PHY degradation, and that JEDEC's absolute maximum is 1.50 V. Taraquin's OCN Zen 3 guide: B-die 'most do 1.5V+ with some airflow'. The voltage is not excessive for these timings: integralfx's scaling example takes good B-die from DDR4-3200 CL14 at 1.35 V to 3733 CL14 at about 1.50 V, and 4 DIMMs plus tRCD 15 add some on top. The risk is heat, not the voltage itself. DRAM power rises with V^2 (+14% from 1.45 to 1.55 V), and there are 4 modules. tRFC is set to the tight B-die value (Taraquin's 3800 range is 256-304 cycles, i.e. 135-160 ns). integralfx: 'tRFC timings are very dependent on temperatures', the ideal range is 30-40 C, and 'you might ... crash while gaming' because the GPU heats the RAM. An OCN user with 4x8 GB single-rank B-die on a 5800X saw 45-50 C under stress and needed a DIMM fan at 3733. This kit probably has no DIMM thermal sensor to read (unverified).
findings.expected_impact: No performance change. The risk is rare heat-induced memory errors, or silent corruption, during long gaming sessions in summer. Long-term degradation risk is low up to 1.55-1.60 V.
findings.risk: Lowering VDIMM can destabilise CL14 or tRFC 288. Raising it adds heat and moves closer to the 1.60 V PHY guidance. The VDIMM figure is estimated from VTT (+/-30 mV) until PC Health confirms it.
sources: https://github.com/integralfx/MemTestHelper/blob/480c3a562c7ce2c4e77fe90efa1c9c7ec686d444/DDR4%20OC%20Guide.md (Maximum Recommended Daily Voltage; Temperatures and Its Effect on Stability)

findings.title: VSOC is fine: true value is 1.11-1.20 V (constant telemetry offset, not load-line droop). The 1.3 V X3D SoC cap is an AM5 rule
findings.current: SMU set point 1.2000 V; SVI2 and pm_table telemetry 1.1125 V. Live test: SoC current went from 10.4 A at idle to 12.8 A under an 8-process memory-copy load, and telemetry stayed at exactly 1.1125 V (87.5 mV gap the whole time). SoC power 12 W, SoC temperature 30-32.5 C.
findings.suggested: No change needed. If you want the true number, read BIOS PC Health 'VCORE SOC', or the IT8688E in4 'Vcore SoC' with the out-of-tree it87 driver. If PC Health shows more than about 1.20 V, trim 'VCORE SOC' (or the DVID offset) until the real value is about 1.15-1.20 V. Keep the real VSOC at or below 1.20 V for daily use. Don't use the AM5 1.3 V figure as a target.
findings.rationale: Why the gap is an offset: if it were load-line droop, a 2.4 A swing at the implied ~8 mOhm would move telemetry about 19 mV (3 SVI2 steps of 6.25 mV). It moved 0 mV. So it is a telemetry offset or a BIOS override, and the real VSOC is somewhere between 1.11 and 1.20 V. Both ends are inside AM4 guidance. Taraquin (OCN Zen 3 guide): SOC 1.05-1.15 V for 1900 FCLK, '4x8gb ram ... often needs more voltage', and 'stay below 1.2v soc and 1.1v iod'. An OCN user on the same board (B550 AORUS PRO, 5800X) with two Viper Steel 4400 kits at 4x8 GB: 'would not run 4 sticks ... with any less than 1.12V vsoc'. integralfx: negative SoC scaling 'typically occurs between 1.15 V and 1.25 V'. Why the X3D cap does not apply: AMD's 'cap on SOC voltage at 1.3V' (HWCooling, 2023-05-03) is the AM5 Ryzen 7000/7000X3D burn-out fix. The 5800X3D's X3D-specific limit is core voltage. Per AMD's Robert Hallock (HWCooling 2022-03-21), the cache die tolerates only about 1.30-1.35 V, so CPU voltage and multiplier are locked, while memory and FCLK overclocking stay allowed. The stacked L3 gets its power through TSVs from the CCD rails (VDDM/RVDD, per Chip Scale Review 2022; seen in a search summary, page not retrieved), not from VDDCR_SOC. VSOC feeds the same 12 nm IOD as a 5800X, so normal AM4 SoC limits apply.
findings.expected_impact: None. Trimming 50 mV would save about 1 W of SoC power, which doesn't matter on a 5800X3D whose games run far below its 142 W PPT.
findings.risk: Lowering VSOC below about 1.10-1.12 V real with 4 DIMMs risks training failures or fabric errors. Above 1.20 V real risks negative scaling and long-term IOD stress.

findings.title: All the cLDO voltage relationships hold. 'VDDP <= VDIMM/2' is not a real rule
findings.current: VDDG IOD 0.9976 V, VDDG CCD 0.9976 V, CLDO_VDDP 0.8973 V, VDDM 0.9504 V, all steady across reads. VSOC 1.1125 V telemetry / 1.20 V set point. CPU VDD18 (IT8792E in4) 1.788 V. VDIMM about 1.53-1.56 V.
findings.suggested: Leave as is. Leave VDDM on Auto: it is the AGESA-managed L3/V-Cache SRAM rail, and nobody tunes it for memory overclocking.
findings.rationale: Each rule against the snapshot: (a) VSOC >= VDDG + about 40 mV. The Stilt (Matisse, quoted on OcUK 2019-07-09 and by integralfx): cLDO_VDDG and cLDO_VDDP 'are regulated from the VDDCR_SoC plane ... minimum drop-out voltage (Vin-Vout) is around 40mV', so the ACTUAL SoC voltage has to be at least that much higher. Headroom here is 115 mV even on the pessimistic 1.1125 V, so this passes. (b) AMD's own rule (Robert Hallock, Community Update #4): 'VDDP cannot be set to a value greater than VDIMM-0.1V (not to exceed 1.05V)'. 0.897 V is far below both limits, so this passes. (c) VDDP < VDDG is a community heuristic, not an AMD rule; 0.897 < 0.998, so it passes anyway. (d) VDDG CCD <= IOD: I found no primary source making this a rule. Common starting points put CCD about 50 mV below IOD (integralfx 0.95/1.05; Taraquin 1.00/1.05; Taraquin's 1900 ranges are CCD 0.85-1.00 and IOD 0.95-1.05). Equal at 1.00 V is within both. (e) 'VDDP <= VDIMM/2': I found no source. Stock JEDEC (VDIMM 1.2 V, AGESA VDDP about 0.9 V) would break it, so it cannot be a real constraint; the real limit is VDIMM - 0.1 V. VDD18 is at its 1.8 V default; Taraquin says below 2.0 V is safe.
findings.expected_impact: None. The rails are internally consistent, and the pm_table readback shows the LDOs reaching their targets.
findings.risk: None from leaving it.

findings.title: The voltages fit FCLK 1867 with 4 single-rank DIMMs well, and no corrected machine-check errors show up
findings.current: FCLK = UCLK = MCLK = 1867 MHz (DPM0 only, 100% residency). VDDG IOD/CCD 1.00/1.00 V, VDDP 0.90 V, VSOC 1.11-1.20 V. Over 3 days of uptime the /proc/interrupts MCE, THR and DFR counters are all 0. The kernel journal kept since 15:44 today has no 'Hardware Error' or 'mce' lines (edac_mce_amd is loaded; earlier journal entries were rotated out).
findings.suggested: Keep 1867. To get the Linux counterpart of Windows WHEA-19, run `journalctl -k -g 'Hardware Error|mce:'` after a long gaming session. Corrected fabric and link errors appear there as corrected machine-check reports. rasdaemon is not installed, so the kernel log is the record.
findings.rationale: Every one of these voltages is inside Taraquin's band for the harder 1900 FCLK target (SOC 1.05-1.15, VDDP 0.8-1.0, CCD 0.85-1.00, IOD 0.95-1.05 V). The Stilt says 1800 FCLK 'should be doable at the default 0.950V' VDDG, so 1.00 V at 1867 leaves margin. 3733 is also already 800 MT/s (+27%) above AMD's official 5800X3D limit for 4x single-rank (DDR4-2933), on a board Gigabyte describes as daisy-chain, i.e. built for 1 DIMM per channel. 3733 is a sensible ceiling for this topology. More voltage won't buy back much margin.
findings.expected_impact: None, since this is the current state. It is a good baseline to restore after the flash.
findings.risk: The MCE evidence only covers about 4 h of retained journal and an unknown workload, so check again after gaming.

findings.title: FCLK 1900 (DDR4-3800) is possible with modest VDDG changes but likely gains under 0.5% fps on an X3D. Skip 1933
findings.current: FCLK 1867 / DDR4-3733 CL14. VDDG IOD/CCD 1.00/1.00, VDDP 0.90, VSOC set 1.20 (1.11 telemetry), VDD18 1.79 V, VDIMM about 1.53-1.56 V.
findings.suggested: Optional, and only after the F19c flash is stable. Try in this order: VDDG IOD 1.05 V (cap 1.10); VDDG CCD 0.95-1.00; VSOC unchanged as long as real VSOC >= IOD + 0.04 V (about 1.09 V) and <= 1.20 V; VDDP 0.90, trying 0.95 or 0.85 only if it fails to train or hits a 'hole'; ProcODT 34-40 Ohm if you set it by hand (Taraquin's 4x8 GB range is 28-48 Ohm); CPU VDD18 +25-50 mV only if errors appear above 1900 (keep it under 2.0 V). Keep VDIMM at or below about 1.55-1.56 V. If 3800 CL14 needs more, use CL15/16 or a looser tRFC rather than more VDIMM. Then check the kernel log for corrected MCEs as in volts-fclk1867-well-matched. If they appear, go back to 1867. Do not try 1933 or higher with 4 DIMMs.
findings.rationale: Taraquin: 'Most Zen 3 can do ... fclk of 1900', but at 1933 or higher 'most will get lots of WHEA19s', and 4x8 GB setups need more SOC and VDDG than 2x8 GB. SkatterBencher #39 found WHEA errors above 1900 on a 5800X3D with 2 DIMMs, and a HardForum 5800X3D hit WHEA at 1933-2000 and could not POST at 1900. The payoff is small. PCGH (2022-05-06) measured a 5800X3D gaining only +1.9% to +3.5% avg fps at 720p for the much larger jump from DDR4-3200 16-18-18 to 3800 16-15-15. Going from tuned 3733 CL14 to 3800 is +1.8% clock, which should be a fraction of that (my estimate: under 0.5%). At GPU-bound settings on a 3080 Ti it is probably nothing. Meanwhile 3800 CL14 with 4 DIMMs would probably push VDIMM toward 1.57-1.60 V, past the daily guidance in volts-vdimm-upper-edge.
findings.expected_impact: About +1.8% fabric and memory bandwidth, and probably under 0.5% CPU-bound fps (estimated from PCGH scaling). No visible gain when GPU-bound.
findings.risk: WHEA-type corrected or uncorrected fabric errors, random reboots at idle (Taraquin), extra VDIMM and heat, and test time spent. The 5800X3D can't trade core overclocking for it, so the gain is purely memory.

findings.title: ProcODT, RTT and CAD-bus values are unknown. Auto works now, but with 2 DIMMs per channel they become the main knobs
findings.current: Not readable. The AOD and APOB buffers live in ACPI NVS, which /dev/mem refuses because of CONFIG_IO_STRICT_DEVMEM. Gigabyte's Auto values for 4x single-rank on this board and AGESA are unverified. The current setup trains and runs at 3733 1T with GDM on.
findings.suggested: Leave them on Auto while 3733 is stable. Capture them once before flashing: boot one time with kernel argument iomem=relaxed (edit the GRUB entry, so it is not persistent) and run scripts/am4_bios_memcfg.py as root. If F19c later trains worse (cold-boot retrains, new errors), enter the captured F16b values by hand under Tweaker > Advanced Memory Settings > Memory Subtimings > 'Data Bus Configuration' / 'CAD Bus Setup Timing' / 'CAD Bus Drive Strength'. The section names are from the Gigabyte manual p.28; the field names inside them are unverified. For a 1900 attempt or a VDIMM/VSOC reduction, community starting points are ProcODT 34-40 Ohm (Taraquin: 28-48 Ohm for 4x8 GB vs 28-37 for 2x8 GB) and drive strengths 24/20/24/24 Ohm (Clk/AddrCmd/CsOdt/Cke). For RTT, one 5800X user with 4x8 GB single-rank B-die settled on Nom/Wr/Park = RZQ/6 / RZQ/3 / RZQ/3 (40/80/80 Ohm), after 2-DIMM RTT values failed.
findings.rationale: With 2 DIMMs per channel, the idle DIMM terminates the bus during every access to the other one. Under JESD79-4 ODT rules that uses RTT_NOM when the controller asserts ODT, otherwise RTT_PARK, with RTT_WR on the target during writes. So RttNom, often disabled on 1-DIMM setups, matters here, and single-DIMM-per-channel recipes don't transfer: the OCN user's 4x8 GB setup failed until RTT was changed from 2-DIMM values. integralfx: 'RTT Wr, Park, and Nom can have a massive impact ... The optimal values will let you clock higher with less memory controller voltage'. 1usmus (via integralfx) suggests ProcODT 28-40 Ohm on Ryzen 3000/5000. AMD's 2017 '60-96 Ohm' advice is from the Zen 1 era and not relevant here. A new AGESA/APCB can change the Auto tables, which is why the F16b values are worth recording first.
findings.expected_impact: None while on Auto at 3733. They decide whether 1900, or lower VSOC/VDIMM, is reachable, and whether F19c trains as well as F16b did.
findings.risk: iomem=relaxed loosens /dev/mem protection for that one boot only. Hand-set termination values that are wrong can cause no-POST, which is recoverable with Load Optimized Defaults or a CMOS clear.
sources: research/aod.md and scripts/am4_bios_memcfg.py (AODT/APOB layout, iomem=relaxed requirement)

findings.title: Record every voltage before flashing F19c, set them explicitly afterwards, and check them from Linux
findings.current: F16b (AGESA 1.2.0.8) values: VSOC set 1.20 V, VDDG IOD/CCD 1.00/1.00 V, CLDO_VDDP 0.90 V, VDIMM about 1.53-1.56 V (VTT 0.763 V). Gigabyte says to 'Load Optimized defaults after updating the BIOS', which puts everything back on Auto.
findings.suggested: Before the flash, photograph Tweaker: 'VCORE SOC' / 'Dynamic VCORE SOC(DVID)' (note whether it is a fixed value or an offset), 'CPU VDD18', 'CPU VDDP', 'DRAM Voltage (CH A/B)', 'DDRVPP Voltage (CH A/B)', 'DRAM Termination (CH A/B)', and CPU/VRM Settings (SoC LLC). Also photograph wherever CLDO VDDP and VDDG CCD/IOD are set (probably the AMD Overclocking/CBS pages; location unverified). After the flash, enter them explicitly instead of trusting Auto. Then run the snapshot plus compare script and check: pm_table SOC set about 1.200, VDDG 0.9976/0.9976, VDDP 0.8973; IT8792E in1 back at 0.763 V (ADC 70), which means the same VDIMM within about 11 mV. If the new SMU firmware changes the pm_table version, use BIOS PC Health 'VCORE SOC' and 'DRAM Channel A/B Voltage' instead. Do not confuse Tweaker 'CPU VDDP' (probably the external board VDDP rail; the reference board's PC Health read 0.924 V) with CLDO_VDDP; this distinction is unverified for this BIOS.
findings.rationale: Auto voltage rules can change between AGESA versions. Taraquin reports AGESA 1.2.0.4 'tends to lock VDDG IOD to 1.00V for some users'. Gigabyte's F16b->F19c changelogs mention no memory changes (research/bios.md), so the risk is silent Auto drift, not a known regression. AMD distinguishes the AGESA CLDO_VDDP from an older external 'VDDP' entry ('This is not the same parameter'), and Gigabyte's Tweaker list and PC Health both show a 'CPU VDDP' separate from the pm_table CLDO_VDDP. The ryzen_smu pm_table and the IT8792E VTT channel are already in the snapshot JSON (hwmon_sensors), so they give an objective before/after check without Windows tools.
findings.expected_impact: Avoids post-flash instability or silent overvolting (e.g. Auto VSOC or VDIMM drifting) and gets back to the known-good 3733 configuration on the first try.
findings.risk: Low. Typing a wrong value can cause no-POST, which is recoverable by CMOS clear. Saved profiles may not carry over between BIOS versions (research/bios.md).
sources: https://download.gigabyte.com/FileList/Manual/mb_manual_b550-aorus-pro-ac_1001_e.pdf (p.28 Tweaker voltage items, p.32 PC Health, p.38 Load Optimized defaults)

review.notes:
The voltages are all within safe limits and well matched to FCLK 1867 with 4 single-rank DIMMs. Two things need attention: VDIMM, estimated at about 1.53-1.56 V, is at the top of the B-die daily range with 4 DIMMs under a hot GPU, and every voltage should be recorded before the F19c flash. Going to 1900 FCLK is possible but gains almost nothing on a 5800X3D. Leave 1933 alone.

**Live checks I ran (read-only, plus a short memory load):**
- **pm_table, 30 samples:** SoC current went from 10.4 A at idle to 12.8 A while 8 processes copied memory. VSOC telemetry stayed at exactly 1.1125 V against a 1.2000 V set point. A fixed 87.5 mV gap that doesn't move with current is an offset or BIOS override, not load-line droop. The real VSOC is therefore somewhere between 1.11 and 1.20 V.
- **One bad pm_table read:** the first read after a pause showed FCLK 1961, SoC set 1.142 V and telemetry 1.041 V. Every read before and after was normal (1867 / 1.200 / 1.1125), so it looks like a mid-update (torn) read. Ignore single-sample outliers when comparing snapshots.
- **VTT:** IT8792E in1 read 763 mV on all 10 samples.
- **Machine-check errors:** the MCE, THR and DFR interrupt counters are 0 after 3 days of uptime, and the kernel journal kept since 15:44 today has no "Hardware Error" lines. The edac_mce_amd module is loaded; rasdaemon is not installed. The non-root `dmesg` read was blocked, so I only had the journal.

**Sources checked directly:**
- Taraquin's OCN Zen 3 guide (Wayback 20230312025707).
- integralfx DDR4 OC guide, commit 480c3a5.
- AMD Community Update #4 (Wayback), source of the "VDDP <= VDIMM-0.1V, max 1.05V" rule.
- The Stilt's Matisse text on cLDO dropout (about 40 mV), as quoted on OcUK.
- HWCooling: the 1.3 V SoC cap is for AM5, and AMD's Robert Hallock gave about 1.30-1.35 V as the 5800X3D cache-die limit.
- PCGH 5800X3D RAM-scaling test.
- Gigabyte B550 AORUS PRO manual, local copy at /tmp/gbman/man_e.txt, for the Tweaker and PC Health item names.
- PR #1036 screenshots, which show the BIOS PC Health names "VCORE SOC" and "DRAM Channel A/B Voltage".

**Unverified:**
- I found no primary source for "VDDG CCD <= IOD" or "VDDP <= VDDG". Both are heuristics, and both are met anyway.
- "VDDP <= VDIMM/2" has no source, and stock JEDEC settings would break it, so it is not a real rule.
- The V-Cache die being powered from VDDM/RVDD comes only from a Chip Scale Review search excerpt; I couldn't retrieve the page.
- Gigabyte's Auto ProcODT, RTT and CAD values for 2 DIMMs per channel are unknown.
- Where CLDO VDDP and VDDG are set in the BIOS is unknown; the manual only lists the Tweaker items.
- Whether Tweaker "CPU VDDP" is the external rail is unconfirmed.
- Whether this kit has a DIMM thermal sensor is unknown.

**Files:**
- Measurement script: /tmp/volts_scripts/socll.py
- Downloaded pages: /tmp/volts_dl/ (Taraquin text t1.txt, integralfx2.md, amd_cu4.txt, ocuk1.txt)

verdicts.reason: Checked and correct: IT8792E in1 read 763 mV on 10 of 10 live samples. in5 (1493 mV) is PM_CLDO12; the Gigabyte manual's PC Health list (man_e.txt L1682) shows PM_CLDO12 as a separate item from 'DRAM Channel A/B Voltage', so it is not VDIMM. The integralfx quotes check out: S8B daily up to 1.55 V (L283), 1.60 V PHY guidance (L277), 1.50 V JEDEC absolute maximum (L274), tRFC and temperature (L306-309). So do Taraquin's 'most do 1.5V+ with some airflow' (t1 L206) and the OCN user's 45-50 C and DIMM fan at 3733 (ocn_5800x L62/L65). The arithmetic holds: (1.55/1.45)^2 = 1.143; tRFC 304/312 at 1866.67 MHz = 162.9/167.1 ns. Three things are overstated. (a) The range is too narrow at the top. The ADC quantises both readings (yours 70 counts, the reference board 62 counts), so 1.380 x 70/63 to 1.380 x 71/62 gives about 1.53-1.58 V, centred near 1.555 V. Plain 2 x VTT reads about 2% low on the reference board (2 x 0.682 = 1.364 vs 1.380 measured). (b) The estimate is only valid if 'DRAM Termination (CH A/B)' is on Auto. The manual (p.28) lists it as a user-settable voltage, and if it is fixed, VTT no longer equals VDDQ/2. (c) 1.55 V is not a hard ceiling. The same integralfx section (L278) says S8B 'should be fine at running 1.60 V daily' with active airflow. There is a real chance PC Health reads 1.56-1.58 V. Lowering VDIMM on a stable 4-DIMM CL14 / tRFC 288 setup to get under 1.56 V trades a real risk of instability for a speculative gain in lifespan. The thermal argument (4 DIMMs, a hot GPU, tight tRFC, no readable DIMM sensor) is the part that holds up.
verdicts.corrected_suggested: 1) Read BIOS PC Health 'DRAM Channel A/B Voltage', and check that 'DRAM Termination (CH A/B)' is on Auto; otherwise the VTT-based estimate means nothing. 2) If the real VDIMM is at or below about 1.60 V, leave it as is. Do not lower a stable configuration just to get under 1.55-1.56 V. Only lower it, 10-20 mV at a time with retesting, if it reads above 1.60 V. 3) Manage temperature instead: get airflow across the DIMMs or add a small fan. Run a heat-soak test (memory test plus GPU load at the same time for at least 1 h). If errors only appear when the RAM is warm, loosen tRFC from 288 to 304-312 (163-167 ns) rather than adding voltage. 4) Do not read in5 (PM_CLDO12) as VDIMM.
verdicts.corrected_impact: No performance change. The benefit is avoiding rare heat-related memory errors in long or summer gaming sessions. At an estimated 1.53-1.58 V, B-die and Zen 3 PHY degradation risk is low, since this is below the community's 1.60 V daily guidance (no AMD source).

verdicts.reason: I re-ran /tmp/volts_scripts/socll.py. SoC current went from 10.33-10.37 A at idle to 12.56-12.70 A under load, and telemetry stayed at 1.1125 V against a 1.2000 V set point (87.5 mV gap) the whole time. A load line of about 8 mOhm would have moved it about 19 mV (3 SVI2 steps), so the reviewer is right that this is not proportional droop. One transient first sample (set 1.1923 V average, telemetry 1.1198 V) had telemetry rising while the set point fell. That suggests the VRM output does not follow the SMU VID, as with a Gigabyte fixed VCORE SOC or a negative DVID offset, plus a small load line. So the real VSOC is more likely about 1.11 V than 1.20 V. The reviewer's bounds (1.11-1.20 V) still hold, and for the dropout check they used the pessimistic 1.1125 V. The Taraquin quotes check out ('stay beliw 1.2v soc and 1.1v iod', t1 L215; 4x8 GB needs more voltage, L207), as do integralfx on negative scaling at 1.15-1.25 V (L352) and the same-board OCN user's 1.12 V floor (ocn L352). The 1.3 V SoC cap belongs to the AM5 Ryzen 7000 burn-out fix, and the 5800X3D's X3D limit is core voltage (Hallock, about 1.3-1.35 V for the cache), so applying normal AM4 SoC limits is correct. Note: if the real VSOC is about 1.11 V, the system is right at the 1.12 V floor one 4-DIMM user on this board reported. That is a reason to record exactly how VCORE SOC is set (fixed or DVID) before the flash, not a reason to change it now.

Every rule checks against the sources. The Stilt's 40 mV cLDO drop-out (ocuk1.txt L201-202): 1.1125 - 0.9976 = 115 mV of headroom. AMD CU#4 says 'VDDP cannot not be set to a value greater than VDIMM-0.1V (not to exceed 1.05V)' (amd_cu4.txt). That text dates from AGESA 1.0.0.6 (2017, Zen 1), but it is still AMD's only statement, and 0.897 V passes it easily. 'VDDP <= VDIMM/2' would indeed fail at stock (1.2/2 = 0.6 V < 0.9 V), so it is not a real rule. The CCD/IOD and VDDP<VDDG relationships are heuristics and are met. One small overstatement: the pm_table cLDO values (0.8973/0.9976/0.9504) are identical to 4 decimals on every read, so they behave like programmed set points rather than measured outputs. 'Readback shows the LDOs reaching their targets' is therefore unproven. With at least 115 mV of headroom over a roughly 40 mV drop-out, they will reach them anyway.

The conclusion (keep 1867) holds, but the evidence given is the wrong evidence. /proc/interrupts MCE counts only #MC exceptions (uncorrected errors). THR fires only when a bank's counter reaches threshold_limit, and that is 4095 here (sysfs threshold_limit=4095; kernel amd.c THRESHOLD_MAX 0xFFF). DFR counts deferred errors. Corrected errors, the Linux counterpart of WHEA-19, are collected by the 300 s poll (check_interval=300) and increment none of those counters. The journal only goes back to 15:44 (kernel lines from 16:15) despite 3 d 1 h of uptime, and it is full of sched_ext and segfault noise. Better evidence that the reviewer missed: kernel amd.c resets each MCA_MISC error counter and sets CntEn at init, and all 117 per-bank 'error_count' files under /sys/devices/system/machinecheck are 0 after 3 d 1 h. The PCIe AER root-port correctable counters are also 0. The workload over those 3 days is unknown, though. Two smaller points. 'Every voltage is inside Taraquin's 1900 band (SOC 1.05-1.15)' is only true if the real VSOC is about 1.11 V; the 1.20 V set point is above that band. 'Gigabyte describes it as daisy-chain' comes only from search snippets (the pages returned 403). The Stilt's '1800 at 0.950 V VDDG' was written about Matisse; it carries over to Vermeer's same 12 nm IOD, but it only loosely supports a 'margin' claim.
verdicts.corrected_suggested: Keep FCLK 1867. After a multi-hour gaming session, check corrected errors three ways: (1) `find /sys/devices/system/machinecheck -name error_count -exec grep -H . {} + | grep -v ':0$'`, which counts per MCA bank since boot (no output means zero); (2) `journalctl -k -g 'Hardware Error|mce:'`, run soon after the session because this journal keeps only a few hours; (3) `grep . /sys/bus/pci/devices/*/aer_rootport_total_err_cor`. Ignore the /proc/interrupts MCE/THR counters for this purpose.
verdicts.corrected_impact: None, since this is the current state and the baseline to restore. The evidence of no errors is stronger than the reviewer stated (3 days of zero bank counters), but it depends on whether any gaming happened in that window.

verdicts.reason: The PCGH data is correct: 5800X3D, 3200 16-18-18 to 3800 16-15-15 1T gave Cyberpunk +2.6%, Greedfall +1.9%, KCD +3.5% and Handbrake 0%. That test used 2x16 GB dual-rank, which is a reasonable stand-in for 2 DIMMs per channel. 3800/3733.3 = +1.79%, and linear scaling gives roughly 0.2-0.4%, so 'under 0.5%' is fair. The Taraquin quotes check out (L87, L204, L207-215). Three corrections. (a) 'VSOC unchanged' is a weak starting point. The real VSOC is probably about 1.11 V, while Taraquin's 1900 test recipe starts at SOC 1.15 V and says 4x8 GB needs more than 2x8. (b) VDDG IOD currently reads exactly 0.9976 V, and Taraquin notes that some AGESA versions lock IOD at 1.00 V. Setting 1.05 V must therefore be checked in pm_table offset 0x228, or the attempt runs at the old value without anyone noticing. (c) If 3800 needs CL15/16 or a looser tRFC with 4 DIMMs, the gain over tuned 3733 CL14 is about zero or negative. The WHEA check should use the sysfs MCA counters, not only the short journal.
verdicts.corrected_suggested: Optional, and only after F19c is stable at 3733. Set the real VSOC to about 1.15 V (cap 1.20 V), VDDG IOD 1.05 V (cap 1.10 V) and CCD 0.95-1.00 V, and keep VDDP at 0.90 V. Confirm in pm_table that IOD actually reads about 1.05 V. Use ProcODT 34-40 Ohm if you set it by hand. Keep VDIMM at or below 1.60 V real. Only keep 1900 if it holds CL14 with the same tRFC. If it needs CL15/16 or more voltage, go back to 1867. After gaming, check the sysfs MCA error_count, the kernel log and AER, and go back to 1867 on any corrected errors. Do not try 1933 or higher.
verdicts.corrected_impact: +1.8% fabric and memory clock. About 0-0.4% CPU-bound fps if CL14 and the tRFC hold, about 0 or negative if timings must loosen. Nothing when GPU-bound at 3080 Ti settings.

verdicts.reason: Most of it checks out. I verified the capture path will work on this machine: /sys/kernel/security/lockdown is [none], Secure Boot is disabled, and the only blocker is CONFIG_IO_STRICT_DEVMEM, which iomem=relaxed lifts. The JEDEC description is right (RTT_NOM when ODT is asserted, RTT_PARK otherwise, RTT_WR on the target during writes). The RZQ arithmetic is right: RZQ = 240 Ohm, so /6 = 40 and /3 = 80. The OCN quote 'For 4 Dimms better to use 6-3-3 on RTTs' is at ocn L60, integralfx's ProcODT 28-40 at L444, and Taraquin's 28-48 for 4x8 GB and DrvStr 24 20 24 24 at L204. Two caveats are missing. (a) research/aod.md L126 says the AOD buffer may be unpopulated or stale until the WMI SMI 0x9D runs, which Linux cannot trigger. APOB is ZenTimings' primary source for ProcODT, RTT and CAD values, and it is not confirmed readable. The capture may therefore return zeros, and Gigabyte's setup screens show 'Auto' rather than the trained values, so photos can't stand in for it. (b) Taraquin's 24/20/24/24 is a general, mostly 2x8 GB recommendation ('If you want to run 1t you often need to change this'). With 2 DIMMs per channel the CAD bus drives two loads, so these values are untested here.
verdicts.corrected_suggested: Leave termination and CAD settings on Auto while 3733 is stable. Before flashing, boot once with iomem=relaxed (a GRUB edit for one boot, or rpm-ostree kargs --append and then --delete) and run scripts/am4_bios_memcfg.py as root. Only trust the output if the AOD and APOB fields are non-zero and the AOD's tCL/tRCD/tRAS match the SMN values (14/15/36). If that capture fails, there is no Linux way to read the Auto values. In that case keep Auto after the flash and judge F19c by cold-boot training and error counters. For a 1900 attempt or a voltage reduction with 4 DIMMs, starting points are ProcODT 34-40 Ohm and RTT Nom/Wr/Park 40/80/80 Ohm (RZQ/6, RZQ/3, RZQ/3). Treat 24/20/24/24 drive strengths as an untested 2x8 GB recipe.
verdicts.corrected_impact: None at 3733 on Auto. The captured values only matter if F19c trains worse than F16b, or for 1900 and lower-voltage attempts.

verdicts.reason: The item names check out against man_e.txt: Tweaker L1449-1451 lists 'VCORE SOC/Dynamic VCORE SOC(DVID)/CPU VDD18/CPU VDDP/.../DRAM Voltage (CH A/B)/DDRVPP Voltage (CH A/B)/DRAM Termination (CH A/B)'; PC Health L1682 lists 'DRAM Channel A/B Voltage', 'VCORE SOC', 'CPU VDDP' and 'DDRVtt A/B'; and L1909 says 'Always load the Optimized defaults after updating the BIOS'. AMD CU#4 does distinguish the external 'VDDP' from CLDO_VDDP. Three corrections. (a) 'Enter them explicitly instead of trusting Auto' can make things worse. Fixing rails that were on Auto on F16b changes how they behave; a fixed DRAM Termination, for example, stops VTT tracking VDIMM/2, and that also breaks the VTT-based VDIMM check. Only fields that were typed in on F16b should be re-entered. (b) The resolution claim is wrong. One ADC count is 10.9 mV of VTT, which is about 22 mV of VDIMM, so the same count of 70 only confirms VDIMM to within roughly ±11 mV (a 22 mV window) and cannot detect a one-step (10 mV) DRAM voltage change. (c) It leaves out the rollback path. research/bios.md says F16b now returns 404 on Gigabyte's server and the board has a single flash chip, so Q-Flash 'Save BIOS to Drive' is the only way back if F19c trains worse.
verdicts.corrected_suggested: Before flashing: (1) save the F16b image with Q-Flash 'Save BIOS to Drive' and save a Setup Profile to USB; (2) photograph the Tweaker voltages, CPU/VRM Settings (SoC LLC), the memory subtiming pages and the AMD Overclocking/CBS pages, noting for each field whether it shows Auto or a typed value; (3) take the iomem=relaxed AOD/APOB capture. After flashing and loading Optimized Defaults: re-enter only the fields that were manual, and leave the Auto ones (especially DRAM Termination and DDRVPP) on Auto. Then run the snapshot and compare scripts and check SOC set about 1.200 V with telemetry about 1.1125 V, VDDG 0.9976/0.9976 V, VDDP 0.8973 V, and VTT count 70. Confirm the exact VDIMM in PC Health 'DRAM Channel A/B Voltage', because the VTT reading only resolves about ±11 mV of VDIMM.
verdicts.corrected_impact: Avoids Auto drift and silent over- or under-volting after the flash, restores the known-good 3733 configuration, and keeps a way back to F16b if F19c trains worse.

missed: Better error evidence that went unused: /proc/interrupts MCE, THR and DFR do not count corrected errors. On this kernel corrected errors are collected by the 300 s poll (machinecheck0/check_interval = 300), and THR only fires at threshold_limit = 4095. The per-bank MCA counters are the right source: kernel amd.c threshold_restart_block() resets ErrCnt and sets MASK_COUNT_EN_HI at init. All 117 /sys/devices/system/machinecheck/**/error_count files read 0 after 3 d 1 h of uptime, and every PCIe AER root-port aer_rootport_total_err_cor reads 0. By contrast, the journal only reaches back to 15:44 (journalctl --list-boots shows just this boot and 45.6 MB of journals) and is full of other messages. That makes the sysfs counters the real long-window, Linux-side WHEA-19 check.

The kernel log does contain faults, and none of them point at memory. The 3 stack traces (16:17-16:18) are sched_ext 'lavd' watchdog stalls ('du ... failed to run for 38.5s'). There are 40+ segfaults from a process named 'single', all with the same signature ('segfault at 0 ip 0000000000000000 ... error 14') spread across every core. That is a deterministic jump to a null pointer in software, not the scattered addresses random bit flips would produce. Anyone reviewing the journal for memory instability should know these are already explained.

The VDIMM estimate assumes Gigabyte's user-settable 'DRAM Termination (CH A/B)' (manual p.28, man_e.txt L1449-1451) is on Auto, i.e. VTT = VDDQ/2. If it was ever set to a fixed value, 2 x VTT says nothing about VDIMM. The reviewer's range also ignores quantisation on both boards (70 vs 62 counts), which widens it to about 1.53-1.58 V.

Rollback safety for the flash: research/bios.md says F16b is no longer downloadable (404) and the board has a single 256 Mbit flash chip. Q-Flash 'Save BIOS to Drive' before updating is the only way back to the known-good F16b memory training if F19c behaves worse. The voltage-restore finding should have included it.

The AOD/APOB capture plan has a gap. research/aod.md L126 says the AOD NVS buffer may only be filled by the firmware on WMI SMI 0x9D, which Linux cannot trigger, and APOB is not confirmed readable. The iomem=relaxed boot can therefore return zeros. Validate the output against the SMN timings (tCL 14 / tRCD 15 / tRAS 36) before relying on it. On the plus side, I confirmed lockdown is [none] and Secure Boot is disabled, so iomem=relaxed itself will work.

VSOC is probably about 1.11 V real, which is right at the 1.12 V floor that a same-board 4x8 GB Viper Steel user reported (ocn_5800x L352). My re-run of socll.py caught a transient sample where telemetry rose (1.1198 V) while the SMU set point fell (1.1923 V), consistent with the VRM ignoring the SMU VID (a fixed VCORE SOC or DVID offset). So the exact form of the VCORE SOC setting (fixed or DVID offset, and its value) is critical to reproduce after the flash. For any 1900 attempt, VSOC should be raised to about 1.15 V rather than left unchanged.

The pm_table 'first read after idle' outliers are a pattern, not one torn read. The reviewer saw FCLK 1961 / set 1.142 V / telemetry 1.041 V, and I saw set 1.1923 V / telemetry 1.1198 V. Both were the first sample after a pause, which looks like the SMU averaging over a long window that includes low-power transitions. Before/after comparisons should drop the first sample or use medians; ram_snapshot.py already uses medians.

findings.title: You are already near the practical memory-OC ceiling for this setup (5800X3D, 4x8 GB single-rank B-die, daisy-chain B550). Subtimings are the only meaningful headroom left.
findings.current: DDR4-3733 CL14-15-15-36-51, 1T with GDM. FCLK = UCLK = MCLK = 1867 MHz. 4x8 GB single-rank, 2 DIMMs per channel on a daisy-chain board. VDIMM is about 1.53-1.56 V, estimated as 2 x the DDRVTT reading of 0.763 V; the 1.2 V in DMI is only the nominal SPD value. VSOC telemetry reads 1.11 V. tRRDS/tRRDL/tFAW are already at the minimum of 4/4/16. Several secondaries look near auto: tRTP 14, tWR 26, tWTRL 12, tRDRDSCL/tWRWRSCL 5/5, tRDWR 10, tWRRD 3, tRDRDDD/tWRWRDD 6/7, tRAS 36, tRC 51, tRFC 288 (154 ns).
findings.suggested: After the BIOS update, restore the current setup as your baseline. Treat two things as the only realistic headroom: Stage A (tighten secondaries/tertiaries at 3733/1867 with no voltage increase) and, optionally, one FCLK step to 1900 (Stage B). Skip anything at 1933 or above, and skip higher primaries or CL14 at 3800 if they need more VDIMM.
findings.rationale: (1) AMD's official limit for the 5800X3D with 4 single-rank DIMMs is DDR4-2933. You are at 3733, which is 27% above spec. (2) 4x8 GB single-rank B-die on Zen 3 typically lands at 3600-3800. One OCN report is a B550 Aorus Pro running two Viper Steel kits at 3800 CL14. (3) Typical Zen 3 FCLK: 1800-1867 is common, 1900 often but not always works, and 1933+ usually throws WHEA-19 errors. Tom's 5800X3D topped out at 3800/1900. SkatterBencher saw WHEA errors on a 5800X3D above 1900. A HardForum 5800X3D had a no-POST hole at 1900. (4) B-die tCL scales roughly linearly with voltage. integralfx's calculator puts DDR4-3733 CL14 at about 1.50 V for a 3200-14 bin. At your estimated 1.53-1.56 V you are already at the top of the B-die daily range (up to 1.55 V per integralfx). Tighter primaries, or CL14 at 3800 on 4 DIMMs, have no voltage margin. (5) What is still loose costs no voltage to tighten: tRTP 14, tWR 26, the SCLs at 5/5, tWTRL 12, the different-DIMM turnarounds 6/7, and tRFC at 154 ns (B-die range is 120-180 ns).
findings.expected_impact: This is an assessment, not a setting change. Total remaining upside is roughly 0-1% in games (see oc-x3d-sensitivity).
findings.risk: None. This is an assessment.

findings.title: The 96 MB L3 makes the 5800X3D much less sensitive to memory: a full 3200-to-3800 jump measured only +1-3.5%, so going from 3733 to 3800 is worth about 0.1-0.4%
findings.current: DDR4-3733 1:1 with tuned primaries, RTX 3080 Ti, gaming on Linux
findings.suggested: Plan for Stage A and Stage B combined to give about +0-1% average FPS in CPU-bound scenes (1080p or lower, high-refresh). At 1440p/4K on a 3080 Ti, expect roughly 0%. Do the tuning only if you enjoy the process, not because you expect a noticeable gain.
findings.rationale:
PCGH (2022-05-06): 5800X3D, RTX 3090, 2x16 GB dual-rank B-die, 664p/720p, comparing DDR4-3200 16-18-18-38 at FCLK 1600 with DDR4-3800 16-15-15-35 at FCLK 1900.
- 5800X3D: Cyberpunk 127.0 to 130.3 fps (+2.6%), Greedfall +1.9%, Kingdom Come +3.5%.
- 5800X: +6.1%, +2.3% and +7.2% in the same games.
- Handbrake: +0.0% on the 5800X3D.

Launch reviews, summarised by 3DCenter/PCGH (2022-04-23), for 3200 vs 3800 on the 5800X3D:
- Tom's Hardware: +1.0% (99th percentile, 7 games, 1080p).
- TechSpot: +1.3% (1% lows, 8 games).
- Quasarzone: +1.4% (average, 5 games).

Those tests changed 600 MT/s plus tRCD 18 to 15 and gained about 1-3.5%. Going from 3733 to 3800 is only +67 MT/s (+1.8% MCLK/FCLK), so scaling proportionally gives about 0.1-0.4% at 720p. The mechanism is that the 3D V-Cache catches most L3 misses. Phoronix found large Linux gains only in workloads that fit in the cache.

Linux: I found no 5800X3D-specific Linux memory-scaling data. Encoding showed 0.0% in PCGH's test. My inference is that only bandwidth-bound HPC or large-array code would see more than 1%.
findings.expected_impact: Games: about 0-1%, with Stage B alone at 0.1-0.4%. Most Linux desktop workloads: below 0.5%. Synthetic tests (AIDA-style latency/bandwidth) will show more than games do.
findings.risk: None. This is an assessment.

findings.title: Stage 0: before tuning anything, re-create and re-validate the exact F16b baseline on F19c
findings.current: All values are known only from F16b (AGESA 1.2.0.8). ProcODT, RTT and CAD-bus values have not been captured. Several timings look like board auto values, for example tRTP 14 and tWR 26.
findings.suggested:
Before flashing:
- Boot once with iomem=relaxed and rerun scripts/ram_snapshot.py to capture ProcODT, RttNom/RttWr/RttPark and CAD drive strengths/setup times.
- Photograph the BIOS voltage pages: DRAM voltage, SoC, VDDG CCD/IOD and VDDP.

After F19c and Load Optimized Defaults, enter everything by hand:
- DDR4-3733 with FCLK 1867.
- Primaries 14-15-15-15-36-51 (tCL-tRCDRD-tRCDWR-tRP-tRAS-tRC).
- tRRDS/tRRDL/tFAW 4/4/16, tWTRS/tWTRL 4/12, tWR 26, tRTP 14, tCWL 14, tRFC 288.
- tRDRDSCL/tWRWRSCL 5/5, tRDWR 10, tWRRD 3.
- tRDRDSC/SD/DD 1/4/6, tWRWRSC/SD/DD 1/6/7, tCKE 1.
- GDM on, 1T, Power Down disabled.
- Explicit VDIMM and VSOC, the same values as on F16b.

Then run the oc-linux-test-protocol sign-off. Use ram_compare.py to check that the trained values match F16b, for example tPHYRDL 26/26 on both channels. Only start Stage A after that.
findings.rationale: No changelog after F16b mentions memory or FCLK, but AGESA 1.2.0.8-to-1.2.0.12 training regressions are unknown, not ruled out (bios.md). Gigabyte says to load Optimized Defaults after flashing, and stored profiles may not carry over. A validated baseline separates BIOS-caused instability from tuning-caused instability. integralfx also advises updating the BIOS before tuning, not during it.
findings.expected_impact: No performance change. It prevents misattributing errors introduced by the new AGESA.
findings.risk: Low. Auto rules on F19c might pick different values for anything you don't set by hand, so set every field you can.

findings.title: Stage A: tighten the near-auto secondaries and tertiaries at 3733/1867, with no voltage increase
findings.current: tRTP 14, tWR 26, tWTRL 12, tRDRDSCL/tWRWRSCL 5/5, tRAS 36, tRC 51, tRFC 288 (154.3 ns), tRDWR 10, tWRRD 3, tRDRDDD 6, tWRWRDD 7, tCWL 14 (= tCL)
findings.suggested:
Change one group at a time. Screen each step for 20-30 minutes and do the full sign-off only at the end. If a step errors, go back to the last passing value.
- A1: tRTP 14 to 8 and tWR 26 to 16, then try tRTP 6 / tWR 12. Keep tWR = 2 x tRTP, and keep both even because GDM is on.
- A2: tWTRL 12 to 10, then 8. tWTRS stays at 4.
- A3: tRDRDSCL/tWRWRSCL 5/5 to 4/4, then 3/3. Stop at 3 with 4 DIMMs. If only one of them fails, run tRDRDSCL one higher.
- A4: tRAS 36 to 30 and tRC 51 to 45 (tRC = tRP + tRAS). Optionally go to 28/43.
- A5: tRFC 288 to 270 (144.6 ns), then 262 (140.3 ns). Don't go below 140 ns with 4 warm DIMMs.
- A6: tRDWR 10 to 9, then 8. tWRRD 3 to 2 (1 is optional). tRDRDDD 6 to 5 and tWRWRDD 7 to 6. Leave the SD values alone.
- A7 (optional): tCWL 14 to 12 (may need tWRRD +1), and tRCDRD/tRP 15 to 14.
- Leave untouched: tCL 14, 4/4/16, tRDRDSC/tWRWRSC 1, tCKE 1, GDM on, 1T, Power Down off. tREFI is not adjustable on AM4.
findings.rationale:
These come from the presets in integralfx's DDR4 OC guide:
- tWR/tRTP: tight 16/8, extreme 12/6. tWR = 2 x tRTP per JEDEC/Micron.
- tWTRS/tWTRL: 4/10, then 4/8.
- SCLs: safe 4/4, tight 3/3, extreme 2/2. Values above 5 hurt bandwidth, and 2 is realistic only on B-die.
- tRAS minimum is tRCD + tRTP, here 15 + 8 = 23, so 30 leaves margin. tRC = tRP + tRAS.
- B-die (S8B) tRFC is typically 120-180 ns. Taraquin gives 135-160 ns at DDR4-3800 (256-304 cycles).
- tREFI is not modifiable on AMD.
- 'DD' is the different-DIMM turnaround, so it applies to your 2-DIMMs-per-channel layout. 'SD' only matters for dual-rank DIMMs.

The gap is real: tRTP 14 and tWR 26 are JEDEC-style values, and the SCLs sit at the bandwidth-penalty edge of 5. None of these changes needs more VDIMM or VSOC.
findings.expected_impact: Synthetic: probably a few percent more read/copy bandwidth and about 1-3 ns lower DRAM latency. That is an estimate; I have not measured it on this system, so benchmark before and after.
