Games on the X3D: at most about 1% average FPS in CPU-bound scenes, and within run-to-run noise at 1440p and above on a 3080 Ti.
findings.risk: Low to moderate. tRFC, SCL and turnaround values that are too tight can cause freezes or silent data corruption, and often only show up when the DIMMs are warm (4 DIMMs next to a ~350 W GPU). Always heat-soak test. Revert at the first error.

findings.title: Stage B (optional): DDR4-3800 at FCLK 1900 with the Stage-A timings. Keep it only if completely MCE-clean, otherwise go back to 1867
findings.current: 3733/1867 1:1:1. VSOC telemetry 1.11 V (pm_table set point 1.20 V), VDDG IOD/CCD 1.00/1.00 V, VDDP 0.90 V, VDIMM about 1.53-1.56 V
findings.suggested:
Only try this after Stage A has passed sign-off.
- Clocks: DDR4-3800 with FCLK 1900, UCLK coupled.
- Timings: keep 14-15-15, tRAS 30, tRC 45. tRFC 266 (140 ns) or 276 (145 ns). All other Stage-A subtimings unchanged.
- VDIMM: unchanged, no more than about 1.55 V set.
- VSOC: whatever makes telemetry (pm_table 0xB4 / SVI2) read 1.10-1.15 V.
- VDDG IOD: 1.00-1.05 V. VDDG CCD: 0.95-1.00 V. VDDP: 0.90-0.95 V.
- Voltage rules: VDDG no higher than actual VSOC minus 0.04 V. VDDP no higher than VDIMM minus 0.1 V, and never above 1.05 V.
- If it fails to train: record the auto ProcODT from Stage 0, then try values in the 28-40 ohm range.
- If it needs CL16 or more VDIMM: return to 3733.
- Pass criteria: zero corrected MCEs during at least 2 hours of FCLK stress, plus about a week of normal gaming.
findings.rationale:
It gains 1.8% MCLK/FCLK. Tom's Hardware's 5800X3D ran 3800/1900 1:1. Taraquin says most Zen 3 chips do 1900, but samples vary:
- HardForum 5800X3D: no POST at 1900, WHEA errors at 1933-2000.
- SkatterBencher's 5800X3D: WHEA above 1900.

4 DIMMs need more SoC voltage; one OCN user reports at least 1.12 V. The Stilt and integralfx report negative scaling at 1.15-1.25 V VSOC on most Ryzen chips. VDDG is an LDO fed from VSOC with about 40 mV dropout. VDDP must stay at or below VDIMM - 0.1 V and at most 1.05 V (AMD, via integralfx). 1usmus suggests ProcODT 28-40 ohm on Ryzen 3000/5000.
findings.expected_impact: About 0.5-1 ns lower latency and about +1.8% bandwidth. Games: about +0.1-0.4% in CPU-bound 720p/1080p, which is not measurable at 1440p/4K.
findings.risk:
Moderate.
- Fabric errors: corrected bus errors can show up as stutter or audio crackle; uncorrected ones cause reboots.
- Higher SoC and VDDG voltages.
- Possible 4-DIMM training failures.
- Hours of testing for a gain within noise.

findings.title: Stage C (DDR4-3866 / FCLK 1933 or higher) and 2:1 'uncoupled' DDR4-4000+ are not worth it on this system
findings.current: Not configured
findings.suggested: Don't pursue FCLK of 1933 or higher, and don't run DDR4-4000+ with UCLK = MCLK/2. If 1900 fails, the right fallback is 1867, not a higher uncoupled speed.
findings.rationale: Taraquin's Zen 3 guide: at 1933 or higher most chips get lots of WHEA-19 errors; the exceptions are some non-X3D 5600X/5700X/5800X on 2-DIMM boards. SkatterBencher's 5800X3D could set 2133, but logged WHEA errors above 1900. Tom's Hardware on the 5800X3D: 'You can get higher with uncoupled memory, but that results in less performance in games.' Your 4 DIMMs on a daisy-chain layout make high clocks harder still. The theoretical extra gain beyond 1900 is under +1.7% clock, which is worth well under 0.5% on an X3D.
findings.expected_impact: Zero or negative for games. A real risk of fabric errors and lost data from unstable writes.
findings.risk: High relative to a benefit of essentially nothing.

findings.title: Keep GDM on with 1T, Power Down off, and all 4 DIMMs. These are already the right choices
findings.current: GDM enabled, 1T, Power Down disabled, BGS disabled / BGS Alt enabled. 4x8 GB single-rank = 2 ranks per channel. tCL 14 and tCWL 14 are both even.
findings.suggested: Leave these alone. Don't chase GDM-off 1T, which needs CAD-bus drive strength and setup-time tuning and is hard with 4 DIMMs. Don't switch to 2T. Don't pull two DIMMs to reach higher clocks.
findings.rationale: integralfx's performance order is: GDM off 1T, then GDM on 1T, then GDM off 2T. GDM-off 1T is 'pretty difficult' and usually needs drive strengths around 60-20-20-24 plus setup-time tuning. With tCL and tCWL already even, GDM forces no rounding penalty here. Two DIMMs per channel give rank interleaving, with twice the bank groups and banks; per integralfx it 'doesn't matter whether the second rank is on the same DIMM or a different DIMM' for the memory controller. Dropping to 2x8 GB would halve capacity to 16 GB, and the X3D would gain almost nothing from the extra clock. Power Down disabled removes tCKE/tXP from the equation, which is integralfx's baseline step 2.
findings.expected_impact: GDM off with 1T might save a fraction of a nanosecond of command latency. On an X3D that is unmeasurable in games (estimate).
findings.risk: None if left as is.

findings.title: There is no VDIMM headroom left, and the DIMM temperature is unknown. Cap VDIMM at 1.55 V, keep SoC at 1.10-1.15 V actual, and test with the case hot
findings.current: VDIMM is estimated at 1.53-1.56 V. That is above the kit's 1.45 V XMP rating and at the top of the B-die daily range. VSOC telemetry is 1.11 V against a set point of 1.20 V; the actual BIOS value is unknown. VDDG IOD/CCD 1.00 V, VDDP 0.90 V. No DIMM temperature sensor is exposed: hwmon shows no jc42 device.
findings.suggested:
- Confirm the actual DRAM voltage in BIOS PC Health. Alternatively, the out-of-tree frankcrawford/it87 driver reads it from the IT8688E's 'DIMM' input.
- Set VDIMM explicitly and keep it at or below 1.55 V for daily use. Don't raise it for Stage A or B.
- Provide airflow over the four DIMMs, for example front intake or a small fan aimed at the slots.
- Run memory tests with the GPU also loaded.
- Keep VSOC telemetry at 1.10-1.15 V. Keep VDDG at or below actual VSOC minus 0.04 V. Keep VDDP at or below VDIMM minus 0.1 V and never above 1.05 V.
findings.rationale:
From integralfx:
- B-die can run up to 1.55 V daily; above that counts as 'extreme' and a RAM fan is recommended.
- Daily VDIMM above 1.60 V is not advisable on Ryzen 3000/5000 because of PHY degradation risk.
- RAM is happiest at about 30-40 C, and tRFC needs grow with temperature.
- 'Stable in a memory test but crash while gaming' is usually case heat from the CPU/GPU, so test with the GPU loaded.

The Stilt: SoC voltage scales negatively between 1.15 and 1.25 V. The cLDO VDDG/VDDP rails are fed from VSOC. The VDIMM estimate comes from the IT8792E's 'DDRVTT AB' input, which reads 70 ADC counts here against 62 counts on a reference board running 1.380 V DRAM.
findings.expected_impact: Stability and longevity rather than performance. Hot B-die is the most likely reason a configuration that passes tests later fails while gaming.
findings.risk: If VDIMM is raised further to force 3800 or tighter primaries, you get more heat and a higher degradation risk for a gain of under 0.5%.

findings.title: How to test memory-OC stability on Bazzite: stressapptest, y-cruncher, OCCT for Linux, memtest86+, a heat soak, then a btrfs scrub
findings.current: No memory stress tools are installed. Karhu is Windows-only. TestMem5 is Windows-only, and how it behaves under Wine is unverified.
findings.suggested:
Quick screen for each Stage-A step (20-30 min): y-cruncher's native Linux stress test with about 85-90% of RAM and the memory-heavy components (FFT, N63, VT3), or the OCCT for Linux memory test.

Sign-off for each stage, all must pass:
- (a) stressapptest, run in a distrobox (the Fedora package exists): stressapptest -M 27000 -s 3600 -W --pause_delay 3600. That is 1 hour on about 27 of 32 GB; setting --pause_delay equal to -s skips the power-spike phase. It must print 'Status: PASS'.
- (b) OCCT for Linux: memory test for 1 hour, plus the 'Large AVX2' CPU test for 1 hour.
- (c) y-cruncher stress for 1-2 hours.
- (d) memtest86+ from a USB stick (memtest.org) overnight, as a complement. It is slow at catching marginal timings, and Secure Boot may need to be disabled (unverified).
- (e) Heat soak: repeat one of (a)-(c) while a game or GPU benchmark loads the 3080 Ti.
- (f) FCLK: 1-2 hours of combined CPU-memory load plus GPU load while watching for MCEs (see oc-linux-mce-detection), then about a week of normal gaming.
- (g) After any crash, or after finishing a stage: sudo btrfs scrub start -B / and btrfs device stats / to catch data that was corrupted when written.

Don't count a TestMem5 pass under Wine as equivalent to the Windows anta777 configs. If you want that reference test, use a spare Windows install.
findings.rationale: integralfx recommends TM5 (anta777), OCCT memory/Large AVX2, GSAT (stressapptest, with exactly that command line) and y-cruncher. It notes that the Large AVX2 test gets harder to pass the more you tune, and that OCCT VRAM plus Prime95 large FFT is good for FCLK. OCCT has had a native Linux build since April 2025, and v17 (stable 2026-06-30) redesigned its memory test. The Fedora repos carry stressapptest, memtest86+, memtester and rasdaemon (packages.fedoraproject.org returned HTTP 200 for each). Bazzite ships distrobox. The root filesystem is btrfs, so a scrub verifies data checksums.
findings.expected_impact: Lets you tell a stable tune from one that only looks fine. Wasted effort and silent data corruption are the main real-world costs of memory OC.
findings.risk: Low. Expect several hours per stage.

findings.title: The Linux equivalent of WHEA-19 is a corrected MCE in the kernel log. This system is already set up to log and decode them; add rasdaemon to keep them
findings.current:
- edac_mce_amd is loaded (initstate 'live'), with dont_log_ce=0, ignore_ce=0 and check_interval=300 s.
- mcelog.service is inactive by design: its unit has ConditionPathExists=!/sys/module/edac_mce_amd/initstate.
- The CPU is family 25, model 33, stepping 2 (19:21:2).
- The kernel log from 16:15 today to now has 0 'Hardware Error' or 'mce:' lines.
- Journal coverage is short, because only ~45.6 MB of journal is stored right now. You raised retention to SystemMaxUse=1G at 17:32 today via /etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/90-retention.conf.
findings.suggested:
- During tests: journalctl -kf | grep -iE 'Hardware Error|mce:|AER'.
- After each test, wait at least 5 minutes, because corrected errors are polled every 300 s. Then run journalctl -k -b -g 'Hardware Error'.
- After a spontaneous reboot: check journalctl -k -b -1, and look early in the new boot's log for 'Machine check events logged'. Errors left in the MCA banks are reported at boot.
- For a persistent record: rpm-ostree install rasdaemon, reboot, sudo systemctl enable --now rasdaemon, then use sudo ras-mc-ctl --summary and sudo ras-mc-ctl --errors.
- Treat any corrected error from the Coherent Station, PIE, NBIO or UMC banks during FCLK testing as a fail and back off FCLK or adjust VDDG/VSOC. Exactly which bank Windows' 'Bus/Interconnect' WHEA-19 maps to is unverified.
findings.rationale: On Windows, high-FCLK instability shows up as WHEA-Logger Event 19, 'Corrected Machine Check, Bus/Interconnect Error'. Linux receives the same MCA records; edac_mce_amd prints them as '[Hardware Error]: Corrected error, no action required.' followed by 'CPU:n (19:21:2) MCx_STATUS[...]' and the bank name. The module's strings include 'Coherent Station' and 'Corrected error, no action required.' This machine exposes the coherent_station_0/1, pie, nbio, umc_0/1 and l3_cache_0-7 banks under /sys/devices/system/machinecheck. Important limitation: these are non-ECC UDIMMs, so DRAM bit errors do not produce MCEs at all. Only fabric, cache and PCIe faults appear, and memory-timing errors are caught only by the test programs.
findings.expected_impact: Gives Linux the same FCLK pass/fail signal that HWiNFO/WHEA gives on Windows. Without it, 1900 FCLK could look stable while it is quietly correcting fabric errors.
findings.risk: None. rasdaemon is a small service; it needs one layered rpm-ostree package and a reboot.

findings.title: After F19c: Curve Optimizer is the only CPU-side knob left. It helps temperatures and sustained clocks, not peak gaming FPS, so tune it separately from RAM
findings.current: F16b with stock X3D limits: PPT 142 W, TDC 95 A, EDC 140 A, CCLK limit 4.45 GHz. Whether F16b offers CO is unverified. Core clocks are locked.
findings.suggested: Do this only after the memory settings are signed off; never tune CO and RAM at the same time. On F19c, try a negative all-core CO starting around -10 to -15, working toward the AMD cap of -30, or per-core. Validate with single- and multi-threaded stress pinned per core (y-cruncher or mprime with taskset) and keep watching for MCEs. Revert any core that throws errors.
findings.rationale: TechPowerUp (2026-08-21): 'Curve Optimizer is available. Modern BIOS versions enable undervolting… AMD artificially caps the offset range at ±30'. The 5800X3D's boost is capped at 4.45 GHz (pm_table CCLK limit), so CO cannot raise peak clocks. It only lowers voltage and heat so the chip holds clocks longer under the PPT/TDC/EDC and thermal limits. Gaming benefits reported by owners are anecdotal: lower temperatures and 'a few' FPS in flight simulators. integralfx: disable CPU overclocks while tuning RAM, because an unstable CPU produces memory-like errors.
findings.expected_impact: Likely lower CPU temperatures and somewhat better sustained multi-threaded clocks. Games: probably about 0-2% (estimate, no controlled review found).
findings.risk: Too much negative CO causes idle or light-load crashes and corrected MCEs on L2/L3 or execution banks. These can be mistaken for memory instability if done at the same time as RAM tuning.

review.notes:
You are already close to the practical ceiling. DDR4-3733 CL14-15-15 at a 1:1:1 FCLK of 1867, with 4x8 GB single-rank B-die on a daisy-chain board at an estimated 1.53-1.56 V VDIMM, is at or near the top of what this combination does. The only real headroom left is:
- **Stage A:** tighten the near-auto secondaries and tertiaries at 3733/1867, with no voltage change.
- **Stage B (optional):** one FCLK step to 1900.

Expected gains on a 5800X3D are about 0-1% in games, and about 0% at 1440p/4K with a 3080 Ti. The best evidence is PCGH's 5800X3D test: a much bigger jump, DDR4-3200 16-18-18 to DDR4-3800 16-15-15, gave only +1.9 to +3.5% at 720p, against up to +7.2% on the 5800X. The launch reviews (Tom's, TechSpot, Quasarzone) measured +1.0 to +1.4%. Stage C (1933 or higher) and 2:1 mode are not worth it.

**Suggested order:**
1. **Stage 0:** capture ProcODT, RTT and CAD values with iomem=relaxed, then flash F19c. Re-enter the full baseline by hand and validate it.
2. **Stage A:** groups A1-A7, sign off.
3. **Stage B (optional):** only if it is completely MCE-clean.
4. **Curve Optimizer:** separately, after the memory work is done.

**Limits of this research:**
- I could not read the OCN Taraquin guide or the WHEA-19 thread directly; overclock.net served a proof-of-work bot challenge. Taraquin's figures come from the verified facts report.
- I could not reach the TechPowerUp 2026 review (bot check), TechSpot (403) or Wayback (offline). The TPU Curve Optimizer quote comes from research/bios.md.
- I found no Linux-specific memory-scaling data for the 5800X3D.
- The synthetic gains for Stage A (a few percent bandwidth, about 1-3 ns latency) are estimates, not measurements. Benchmark before and after.
- The exact MCA bank that Windows reports as WHEA-19 'Bus/Interconnect' on Linux is unverified.
- The pm_table shows VSOC set to 1.20 V but telemetry at 1.11 V. The real BIOS value needs checking in BIOS.

**Checked live on this system:**
- edac_mce_amd is loaded and corrected errors are logged (dont_log_ce=0); they are polled every 300 s.
- mcelog is intentionally inactive.
- The kernel log since 16:15 today has zero MCE lines, but that only covers about 3.5 hours. Journal retention was raised to 1G at 17:32 today.
- No DIMM temperature sensor is exposed.
- distrobox is present, and the Fedora repos carry stressapptest, rasdaemon and memtest86+.

**Local copies:**
- integralfx DDR4 OC guide: /tmp/ocdl_gh/ddr4guide.md
- Tom's Hardware pages as text: /tmp/ocdl_toms/*.txt
- HTML-to-text helper: /tmp/ocscripts/h2t.py

verdicts.reason: Mostly holds. 3733/2933 = 1.273, so +27% over AMD's 4x1R spec is correct. The integralfx calculator line ("DDR4-3733 CL14 at 1.50 V" for a 3200-14 bin) is quoted accurately (/tmp/ocdl_gh/ddr4guide.md L229), as is the S8B 120-180 ns tRFC table. Two things are overstated. (1) "No voltage margin": the same guide puts S8B "Up to 1.55" as daily (L283), but also says "H8D, M8E, M16B and S8B *should* be fine at running 1.60 V daily ... recommended to have active airflow" (L278), and gives 1.60 V as the Ryzen 3000/5000 PHY limit (L277). So there is roughly 40-70 mV of technical headroom; it is just not worth spending on this X3D. (2) The finding's own evidence (an OCN B550 Aorus Pro with two Viper Steel kits at 4x8 GB 3800 CL14) shows 3800 CL14 is reachable on this exact board and kit, so 'near the ceiling' should not read as 'at it'. It also conflicts with Stage A7, which tightens primaries (tRCD/tRP 14) while this finding says tighter primaries have no margin. Finally, the current 3733 config has never been validated: no test run is recorded, and the zero-MCE window covers only about 3.5 h of journal. The 'baseline' is assumed, not proven.
verdicts.corrected_suggested: Keep the assessment, with these changes. The ceiling is roughly 3733-3800 CL14 on this board and kit. VDIMM has about 40-70 mV of technical headroom up to the 1.60 V Ryzen PHY / S8B limit (integralfx L277-278), but it is not worth using on an X3D. Drop primary tightening (A7) from the no-voltage stage, or label it as possibly needing VDIMM/VSOC. Prove the current config stable before calling it the baseline.
verdicts.corrected_impact: Assessment only. Remaining upside is about 0-1% average FPS; see the 1%-low note on oc-x3d-sensitivity.

verdicts.reason: I fetched PCGH and checked the averages. 5800X3D, 3200 16-18-18-38 to 3800 16-15-15-35: Cyberpunk 127.0 to 130.3 (+2.6%), Greedfall 157.5 to 160.5 (+1.9%), KCD 63.7 to 65.9 (+3.5%). The 5800X gained +6.1/+2.3/+7.2%. Handbrake 5.19 to 5.19. Tom's 3800/1900 quote is verified in /tmp/ocdl_toms/old4.txt L568. Two corrections. (a) PCGH does not state FCLK, so 'FCLK 1600 vs 1900' is an assumption; 1:1 is likely but unverified. (b) The finding ignores the P1 (1% low) column, which moves much more on the X3D: Cyberpunk P1 81.8 to 87.9 fps (+7.5%), KCD 38.2 to 39.1 (+2.4%), Greedfall 115.6 to 117.1 (+1.3%). findings.title: ram_snapshot.py stops completely if ryzen_smu doesn't expose pm_table; the README's "pm_table skipped, timings still work" fallback doesn't exist
findings.current: `pm_snapshot()` runs `struct.unpack("<I", rd(f"{SMU}/pm_table_version", True)[:4])` and `len(raws[-1])` with no guard. `rd()` returns None on OSError, and `main()` calls `pm_snapshot()` before `smn_snapshot()`. The README says that if the new SMU firmware changes pm_table_version, the pm_table fields are skipped and the SMN timings still work.
findings.suggested: Guard `pm_snapshot()`. If `rd(pm_table_version)` or `rd(pm_table)` returns None, return `({'version': None, 'size': 0, 'known_layout': False, 'fields': {}, 'error': 'ryzen_smu exposes no pm_table (see dmesg: Unknown PM table version)'}, b'')`, and drop None samples from `raws`. Then the SMN/UMC timing read, which doesn't depend on SMU firmware, still runs. Optionally also save `dmesg | grep -i ryzen_smu` into raw/.
findings.rationale: In ryzen_smu, `drv.c` (amkillam master, ~L378-405) creates the pm_table, pm_table_size and pm_table_version sysfs files only if `smu_read_pm_table()` succeeds at probe. In `smu.c`, a Vermeer table version the driver doesn't know falls to `UNKNOWN_PM_TABLE_VERSION`, which returns SMU_Return_Unsupported and logs "Unknown PM table version" (~L960-995, ~L1270). The leogx9r fork does the same (smu.c L809-843, L957). So in exactly the case the README covers, a new table version, the files are missing, `rd()` returns None, and the script raises TypeError before it reads any UMC register.
findings.expected_impact: Unlikely to trigger on F19c (see bios-smu-pmtable-stable). If it does trigger, there is no post-flash snapshot or compare until the code is fixed.
findings.risk: None. Read-only code change.

findings.title: F19c ships Vermeer SMU 56.78.0 (you run 56.74.0); its list of pm_table versions matches 56.76's and includes 0x380905, so the table layout should stay the same
findings.current: SMU firmware 56.74.0, pm_table 0x380905 (0x5D0 bytes). Microcode 0xa201211, which Linux loads from linux-firmware (microcode_amd_fam19h.bin, patch dated 2024-09-13).

Check with `cat /sys/kernel/ryzen_smu_drv/version` and `od -An -tx4 -N4 /sys/kernel/ryzen_smu_drv/pm_table_version`. Sanity-check the result: FCLK_MHz should equal FCLK_DPM0_MHz, and VSOC_set_V should match your BIOS VCORE SOC. If you save the F16b image (bios-backup-and-flash-order), run /tmp/smuparse_scripts/psp.py and dumparr.py on it to confirm 56.74 has the same array.
findings.rationale: I parsed the PSP directories in the official images. The Vermeer SMU blob ($PS1 header, version at 0x60) is 56.76.0 in F17, F18b, F18d, F18g, F18 and F19a, and 56.78.0 in F19c. After zlib decompression, each SMU blob contains the same 11-entry array: 0x380805, 0x380005, 0x380105, 0x380205, 0x380305, 0x380405, 0x380905, 0x380505, 0x380605, 0x380705, 0x380B05. The table version is picked by core count (leogx9r smu.c comments: 0x380905 = 8-core). Your 56.74 already picks 0x380905, and the array is unchanged, so the SMU should keep reporting 0x380905. That is an inference; I did not disassemble the selection code. ZenStates-Core PowerTable.cs L293-300 and ryzen_smu know every entry except 0x380B05. The UMC timings are read from hardware registers over SMN and are not affected by firmware.
findings.expected_impact: The pm_table fields (FCLK/UCLK/MCLK, VSOC set and telemetry, VDDP, VDDG, PPT/TDC/EDC) stay directly comparable between F16b and F19c.
findings.risk: Small chance the SMU picks 0x380B05 or another table, in which case ryzen_smu disables pm_table (see bios-snapshot-pmtable-crash).

review.notes:
The single most useful step left before flashing is one more F16b boot with iomem=relaxed and a new snapshot (bios-preflash-apob-baseline). It records the ProcODT, RTT and CAD bus values F16b actually applies. If those settings are on Auto the BIOS screens just say "Auto", and the information is gone for good once you flash.

**SMU firmware and pm_table** (from the official images in /tmp/gbzips):
- The Vermeer SMU goes from 56.74.0 (what you run now) to 56.76.0 in F17 through F19a and 56.78.0 in F19c.
- Each SMU blob has an 11-entry list of pm_table versions. The list is identical in 56.76 and 56.78 and includes 0x380905, so your table version and its offsets will very likely stay the same.
- One entry, 0x380B05, is unknown to ryzen_smu and ZenStates-Core.
- F19c's BIOS microcode is 0xa201213 (dated 2024-12-05). The 0xa201211 you see now comes from linux-firmware.
- Expected differences in the compare: smu_fw, microcode, and BIOS version/date. The UMC timings are read straight from hardware registers, so the firmware can't change how they are read.

**Bug in the snapshot script.** ram_snapshot.py crashes with a TypeError if ryzen_smu doesn't create the pm_table files, and that is exactly what the driver does when it meets an unknown table version. The README says the pm_table part is skipped and timings still work, but that fallback doesn't exist. Guard pm_snapshot() before you flash.

**Checked on this machine:**
- ReBAR is off (BAR1 256 MiB) and CSM looks enabled (legacy BBS boot entries).
- fTPM is on, the root disk is not encrypted, and Secure Boot is off in Setup Mode with one MOK key enrolled.
- IOMMU is on, SVM is off, the C6 idle state is present, and amd-pstate-epp is active.
- No machine-check errors in the current boot. The journal only keeps the current boot.
- Both visible USB drives are unsuitable for Q-Flash: the Samsung T5 is exFAT and the 64 GB JetFlash is your Tails stick.

**Menu names.** Checked against Gigabyte manual Rev 1001 and the F19c setup strings, including F12 screenshot to a FAT16/32 stick, Ctrl+S memory info, Save/Load Fan Profile (F3/F4), Re-Size BAR Support, PBO Limits, Curve Optimizer, VDDG/VDDP Voltage Control, SoC/Uncore OC Mode, and DDR CH(A/B) Voltage Loadline Calibration. Which page the PBO, Curve Optimizer and VDDG items sit on (Tweaker or Settings > AMD Overclocking) is not verified.

**Not verified:**
- Whether you can downgrade from F19c back to F16b. Capsule BIOS has existed since F14, and I found no anti-rollback statement either way.
- Whether Curve Optimizer is in your F16b. Forum reports say AGESA 1.2.0.8 BIOSes exposed it on Gigabyte B550, so check your F16b screens.
- Memory or FCLK regressions in 1.2.0.B through 1.2.0.12: I found no reports either way.
- That the RTX 3080 Ti VBIOS supports ReBAR.

**Suggested order:**
1. iomem=relaxed snapshot on F16b.
2. F12 screenshots of every page in the checklist, Save Profiles to USB, Save Fan Profile.
3. Q-Flash > Save BIOS to Drive on a separate FAT32 stick.
4. Load Optimized Defaults, then flash F19c.
5. Load Optimized Defaults again and boot once at stock.
6. Re-enter settings: voltages first, then speed and FCLK, primaries, subtimings, then ProcODT/RTT/CAD pinned to the F16b values.
7. Snapshot (with iomem=relaxed) and run ram_compare.py, then a stability test.
8. Only after that, as separate steps, ReBAR and Curve Optimizer.

Scripts I wrote for this are in /tmp/smuparse_scripts/: psp.py, smublob2.py and dumparr.py for the SMU and pm_table analysis, and hii.py for the BIOS setup strings.

verdicts.reason: Doing a capture boot is the right call, but four parts of the finding are overstated or missing. (1) The claim that these Auto values are 'most likely to change between 1.2.0.8 and 1.2.0.12' has no evidence behind it. Gigabyte's changelogs after F16b, and AMD bulletins SB-7005, 7014, 7027, 7033, 4011 and 7064, are all security-only. (2) 'Gone for good' ignores the reviewer's own Save BIOS to Drive step: if that image can be reflashed (unverified), you can still recapture on F16b. (3) The research note is outdated. The AML half of am4_bios_memcfg.py already ran on real hardware: snapshot.md shows SSDT3, base 0xBD0BE018 and 105 fields with offsets that agree. Only the /dev/mem reads are untested. (4) The capture as written would throw data away. ram_snapshot.py stores only the decoded text, and am4_bios_memcfg.py prints only MEM type-2 values plus the first 0xCC bytes of the AOD buffer. ZenStates-Core at the same pinned commit (869b7e8, Hardware/Apob/) decodes much more from the APOB: DDR4 MR0-MR6 (ApobDdr4ModeRegisters.cs gives RttNom/RttWr/RttPark, DRAM output impedance and starting VrefDQ, documented as 'Summit Ridge to Vermeer') and per-slot 512-byte SPD copies (ApobDimmSpd.cs, MEM type 17). The firmware memory map has a further trap. /sys/firmware/memmap shows ACPI NVS at 0xA200000-0xA20DFFF (0xE000 bytes) followed by System RAM at 0xA20E000. /dev/mem refuses System RAM even with iomem=relaxed, and read_mem returns EPERM for the whole request. So if the APOB TableSize is over 0xE000, the script's single read_phys(a, tsize) call fails and only 'error: PermissionError' is printed. I confirmed APOB is at 0xA200000: the BIOS directory entry type 0x61 has dst=0xA200000 in F19c. Its size is unknown. (5) In F19c, ProcODT and RTT can only be edited after 'Data Bus Configuration User Controls' is set to Manual (string present in F19c). (6) The APOB MEM type-2 arrays hold one value per channel. On 2 DIMMs per channel they cannot show per-DIMM RTT if the Auto tables use different values per slot (unverified); the MR words are the better source for that.
verdicts.corrected_suggested: Before the capture boot, patch am4_bios_memcfg.py/ram_snapshot.py in three ways. (a) Write the raw AODT buffer (0x220C bytes at 0xBD0BE018) and the raw APOB to snapshot raw/ files. (b) Read the APOB one 4 KiB page at a time, or clamp the read to 0xE000 bytes, and stop at the first EPERM instead of aborting. (c) Keep the decoded print as it is. Boot F16b once with iomem=relaxed. A one-time GRUB 'e' edit is simplest: Bazzite hides the GRUB menu, so hold Shift or press Esc at boot. That also avoids creating and deleting an ostree deployment while update 44.20261023 is staged. Decode the MR0-MR6 words and SPD records offline later, following ZenStates-Core 869b7e8. Keep the BIOS screenshots as the fallback. On F19c, the cleanest option is one capture boot with ProcODT/RTT/CAD left on Auto, then compare. Pin the F16b values only if they differ or 3733 fails; otherwise pin them all, after setting 'Data Bus Configuration User Controls' to Manual.
verdicts.corrected_impact: Diagnostic only, with no speed change. Whether 1.2.0.12's Auto ODT/CAD values differ from 1.2.0.8's is unknown, not 'most likely'. The raw dumps also capture the SPD/XMP data of all four DIMMs, which would settle the two-kits question that is otherwise listed as not available.

verdicts.reason: Checked against amkillam/ryzen_smu master. In drv.c L378-405, the pm_table, pm_table_size and pm_table_version attributes are added only when smu_read_pm_table() returns OK. In smu.c, the Vermeer/Chagall switch (L959-994) knows only 0x2D0803, 0x2D0903, 0x380005, 0x380505, 0x380605, 0x380705, 0x380804, 0x380805, 0x380904 and 0x380905. Any other version reaches UNKNOWN_PM_TABLE_VERSION, returns SMU_Return_Unsupported and logs 'Unknown PM table version' (L1272-1275). In ram_snapshot.py, rd(binary=True) returns None on a missing file, L99 then does None[:4] and raises TypeError, and main() calls pm_snapshot() (L237) before smn_snapshot() (L238). The rest of the proposed fallback works: zen3_ddr4_decode.decode_umc handles pm_mclk_mhz=None (L150), and render_md/ram_compare cope with empty fields. One addition: also guard a transient OSError on an individual pm_table read (rd returns None, then len()/unpack_from fail).

I re-ran smublob2.py and dumparr.py on all seven official images. The SMU is 56.76.0 in F17, F18b, F18d, F18g, F18 and F19a, and 56.78.0 in F19c. All of them contain the same 11-entry array with 0x380905 at the same index. ucode.py confirms F19c carries 0xa201213 (dated 2024-12-05) and F17 carries 0xa20120e. linux-firmware in the booted deployment, and in the staged one, has 0xa201211 (2024-09-13) for A20F12. So expecting microcode to change to 0xa201213 is correct. One claim is wrong: 'ZenStates-Core and ryzen_smu know every entry except 0x380B05'. PowerTable.cs L293-300 and the ryzen_smu smu.c Vermeer switch both lack 0x380105, 0x380205, 0x380305 and 0x380405 as well as 0x380B05, so 5 of the 11 entries are unknown, not 1. The SMU 56.74 array is unverified because the F16b image is not available. The 'picked by core count' mapping is also unverified; the actual evidence is that this 5800X3D already reports 0x380905 on 56.74. 0x380B05 sits last in the array, so it may belong to a SKU added after F16b. That leaves a real but small chance the SMU switches tables, and the pm_table would then disappear.
verdicts.corrected_suggested: Keep the expectations: smu_fw 56.74.0 to 56.78.0, microcode to 0xa201213, pm_table staying 0x380905 (likely, not certain). Fix the guard in ram_snapshot.py first (bios-snapshot-pmtable-crash). Note that /sys/kernel/ryzen_smu_drv/pm_table_version is world-readable (0444), so the od check does not need sudo. If you save the F16b image, run dumparr.py on it to compare the 56.74 array.
verdicts.corrected_impact: pm_table comparability between F16b and F19c is likely but unproven. If the table changes, only the clock, voltage and limit fields are lost; the SMN timings are unaffected.

verdicts.reason: The menu names check out. Manual Rev 1001 (/tmp/gbman/man_e.txt) has F12 Print Screen, Ctrl+S, the five Memory Subtimings sub-pages, the full voltage list including DRAM Termination (CH A/B), PC Health 'DDRVtt A/B/DRAM Channel A/B Voltage/PM_CLDO12', CSM Support, Save/Load Profiles and 'Always load the Optimized defaults'. The F19c strings I extracted with hii.py match: 'F12 : Print Screen(FAT16/32 Format Only)', Re-Size BAR Support, Curve Optimizer, VDDG/VDDP controls, SoC/Uncore OC Mode. Three gaps need correcting. (1) The checklist captures AMD CBS only 'if you ever changed something there'. DF Cstates and APBDIS exist in F19c, directly affect stability at 1867 FCLK, and are reset by Optimized Defaults; the user may not remember changing them. (2) 'Data Bus Configuration User Controls' (an F19c string) is missing, and it decides whether the ProcODT/RTT values shown are manual. (3) 'PC Health is the only way to read VDIMM' is overstated: the AOD buffer's MemVddio/MemVtt (in mV) from the iomem=relaxed boot, and the out-of-tree frankcrawford it87 driver (supports IT8688E), are two more ways.
verdicts.corrected_suggested: Use the same checklist, plus: AMD CBS > DF Common Options (DF Cstates, APBDIS, Fixed SOC P-state) and NBIO/SMU Common Options pages, 'Data Bus Configuration User Controls', and the DRAM Termination (CH A/B) value, which decides whether the it8792 in1 VTT proxy means anything. Take the screenshots on the same FAT32 stick you use for Save BIOS to Drive.

verdicts.reason: Verified locally. lsblk shows sda1 vfat 'Tails' 8G with sda2 crypto_LUKS (the JetFlash), and sdb2 exfat 'SamsungT5'. The Q-Flash UEFI guide text says 'The Save BIOS to Drive option allows you to save the current BIOS file' and 'Q-Flash only supports USB flash drive or hard drives using FAT32/16/12'. F19c strings include 'Save BIOS to Drive' and 'Not able to save BIOS file successfully'. The X570 features guide confirms the GIGABYTE.bin rename. The Wayback JSON ties capsule BIOS support and the fTPM default to the 1.2.0.5 release, labelled F14 in the JSON, which is before F16b either way. The reviewer correctly says that reflashing the saved image or downgrading is unverified; I found only forum anecdotes about Gigabyte 'prevent roll back', none official for this board.

The arithmetic holds: 0.763 V is 70 steps of 10.9 mV, and at a ratio of 2.02, 1.45 V gives about 65-66 steps and 1.20 V about 54-55. The LHM mapping (in1 = 'DDRVTT AB') is confirmed in SuperIOHardware.cs L2930-2946. But VTT is not a fixed VDIMM/2 on this board. 'DRAM Termination (CH A/B)' is its own adjustable voltage in the Tweaker list (manual p.28). The proxy holds only while DRAM Termination is on Auto (tracking VDDQ/2). If it was set manually on F16b, or gets mistyped on F19c, in1 follows the termination set point, not VDIMM. In that case the current '1.53-1.56 V' estimate and the post-flash check would both be wrong. 2 x in1 also reads about 1-2% below the real VDIMM (reference ratio 2.02, not 2.00). That is harmless for a relative diff, but it should not be shown as an absolute VDIMM.
verdicts.corrected_suggested: Add the in1 diff to ram_compare.py, flagging a change of 2 ADC steps or more (about 22 mV on VTT). Name it 'VTT (DDRVTT AB)'. If you also show VDIMM_est = 2.02 x in1, label it valid only when DRAM Termination = Auto. Screenshot DRAM Termination (CH A/B) together with PC Health 'DRAM Channel A/B Voltage' and 'DDRVtt A/B' on both BIOSes. When the iomem=relaxed boot works, also record the AOD MemVddio/MemVtt mV values.
verdicts.corrected_impact: Catches a wrong VDIMM or VTT after re-entering settings, as long as DRAM Termination is on Auto. Otherwise it only catches VTT changes.

verdicts.reason: I verified each proxy on this machine. efibootmgr shows BBS(HD) entries Boot0001, 0003 and 0008, so CSM is enabled. nvidia-smi reports BAR1 256 MiB, and lspci shows Region 1 at d0000000 [size=256M]. /sys/class/tpm/tpm0 is version 2 and /sys/class/iommu/ivhd0 exists. /dev/kvm is absent and the 'svm' flag is missing from /proc/cpuinfo while 'npt' is present, which is stronger evidence that SVM is disabled by BIOS. The cpuidle states are POLL, C1 and C2 (C2 desc 'ACPI IOPORT 0x414'). amd-pstate-epp is active with boost=1. mokutil reports SecureBoot disabled and Setup Mode. The manual defaults quoted (SVM Disabled, Above 4G Disabled, CSM Enabled, IOMMU Auto, Global C-state Auto) are on manual pp.27, 30, 32 and 37. Rev 1001 dates from 2020, so F19c defaults may differ, which is one more reason to fingerprint. Side note: the user is in the 'libvirt' group but SVM is off. If they want KVM VMs, they should turn SVM Mode on while re-entering settings.

Confirmed on the machine: BAR1 is 256 MiB, BBS entries mean CSM is on, and Bazzite boots from the UEFI shim entry Boot0006. No disk carries a legacy-only OS: lsblk shows only the nvme ESP/btrfs, the Tails USB and the exFAT T5, and the BBS entries are just the same devices. F19c contains 'Re-Size BAR Support', and the manual says Secure Boot needs CSM Disabled. Phoronix (Sept 2021, RTX 3060 Ti/3070/3090 with a 2021 driver) found gains in DiRT Rally 2.0 and Total War: Three Kingdoms and flat results in many other titles, which matches the claim. Caveats: that data is old and from other SKUs, and on Linux ReBAR is not whitelisted per game as it is on Windows. Measure per title, since a small regression in some titles is possible. NVIDIA said the 3080 Ti would support ReBAR from launch, and the BAR1 check confirms it either way.

F19c strings include All Core and per-core Curve Optimizer Sign/Magnitude. Forum reports (TechPowerUp threads; an Aorus B550 Elite V2 user on F16b beta with 1.2.0.8: 'surprised to see PBO was back') support CO/PBO showing up in Gigabyte's AGESA 1.2.0.8 BIOSes. TechPowerUp's 2026 review cites the ±30 cap. ZenStates-Core Zen2Settings.cs L35 really has 'Rsmu.SMU_MSG_GetDldoPsmMargin = 0x7C; // Not sure', and Zen3Settings overrides only the MP1 Set messages (0x35/0x36), so the warning against reading CO through the SMU stands. The staged approach (memory first, then CO from -10 toward -20/-30 with per-core testing) is sound. The expected 0-2% gaming impact is plausible for a 4.45 GHz-capped X3D paired with a 3080 Ti.

The direction is right: the post-F16b changelogs and AMD bulletins are security-only, and treating unexplained diffs as Auto drift is sensible. But the list of fields to 'pin back' includes things you can't set. tPHYRDL (and tPHYWRL/tPHYWRD) are PHY latencies set or derived by training. tPHYRDL commonly differs between channels or boots after retraining, so a change there is expected, not a setting to restore. F19c has no setup strings for tSTAG or PHYRDL; it does have tRDRDSD/tRDRDDD, TwrwrDd and tRFC/tRFC2/tRFC4. So tSTAG and tPHYRDL can't be pinned from Gigabyte setup either. Note also that edac_mce_amd is loaded and the MCE poll interval is 300 s, so corrected-error checks need runs well over 5 minutes. Journal retention is fine: /etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/90-retention.conf (SystemMaxUse=1G) was added today and overrides Bazzite's 50M, so the 'journal keeps only the current boot' remark is now out of date.
verdicts.corrected_suggested: Diff everything, but sort the differences into two groups. (a) BIOS-settable values, which you pin back: tRDRDSD/DD, tWRWRSD/DD, tRFC*, GDM/Cmd2T, VSOC/VDDG/VDDP, and ProcODT/RTT/CAD with Data Bus User Controls set to Manual. (b) Trained or derived values, which you only note: tPHYRDL, tPHYWRL, tPHYWRD, tSTAG. A tPHYRDL difference between channels is a training-quality hint, not a setting. Validate with stress runs of 30 minutes or more, then check `journalctl -k -b | grep -iE 'mce|hardware error'` (edac_mce_amd decodes corrected errors).
verdicts.corrected_impact: No performance change expected. It avoids chasing PHY latency differences you cannot set.

verdicts.reason: Verified. The root filesystem is plain btrfs on nvme0n1p3; the only LUKS volume is sda2 (Tails). There is no Windows/BitLocker partition. mokutil reports 'SecureBoot disabled' and 'Platform is in Setup Mode', and the enrolled MOK keys are the Fedora CA and the 'ublue kernel' key. tpm0 is TPM 2.0. /usr/lib/efi/shim/16.1-7 ships BOOTX64.EFI and fbx64.efi, and efibootmgr shows the Bazzite and Fedora entries on the ESP. F19c contains the 'New CPU installed, fTPM/PSP NV corrupted or fTPM/PSP NV structure changed.' prompt. With Secure Boot off, the MOK list does not matter for loading the NVIDIA modules. Unverified: /etc/crypttab and /etc/credstore.encrypted are root-only, so TPM-sealed systemd credentials can't be fully ruled out (unlikely). The reviewer already noted this limit.

missed: Raw firmware buffers aren't saved, so the capture boot can't be re-parsed later. am4_bios_memcfg.py prints only decoded MEM type-2 values and the first 0xCC bytes of the AOD buffer, and ram_snapshot.py stores that text and nothing else. ZenStates-Core at the same pinned commit 869b7e8 (Hardware/Apob/ApobDdr4ModeRegisters.cs, ApobDimmSpd.cs, ApobDmiInfo.cs, ApobBootInfo.cs) pulls much more from the same APOB: the DDR4 MR0-MR6 words (RttNom/RttWr/RttPark, DRAM Ron, starting VrefDQ; 'Summit Ridge to Vermeer'), the 512-byte SPD of every slot (MEM type 17), and the memory voltage (SMBIOS type 8). Dump the full APOB and the 0x220C-byte AODT (which ends in 16 x 0x214 SPD copies at 0xCC) to raw/ during the iomem=relaxed F16b boot. That also captures the SPD/XMP contents and serial/date data of all four DIMMs, which is listed as NOT AVAILABLE, and settles the two-kits question.

The APOB read can fail even with iomem=relaxed. /sys/firmware/memmap shows 0xA200000-0xA20DFFF as ACPI NVS (only 0xE000 bytes) and 0xA20E000 onward as System RAM. x86 devmem_is_allowed refuses System RAM above 1 MiB whatever the iomem setting, and read_mem returns EPERM for the whole request if any page is refused. apob() calls read_phys(a, tsize) once, outside any try. So any TableSize over 0xE000 loses the whole APOB, and the outer handler prints only 'error: PermissionError'. The F19c BIOS directory confirms the APOB destination (type 0x61, dst=0xA200000) but gives size 0. Read page by page or clamp to 0xE000.

A Bazzite update is already staged and will be booted on the next reboot. `rpm-ostree status` shows pending 44.20261023 (249 packages, including a ryzen_smu/kmod rebuild, linux-firmware and amd-ucode 20260916 -> 20261019, and kmod-zenergy). uupd.timer runs again on 2026-10-25 at 04:07. I checked that the kernel (7.2.9-ogc3.1) and the Vermeer microcode (0xa201211) are the same in that deployment, so the confound is small for now. But the snapshot doesn't record the ostree deployment, and a later automatic update could change kernel or ryzen_smu between the F16b and F19c captures. Pause uupd until the compare is done, take the F16b baseline on the deployment you will also use on F19c, and add the booted deployment checksum/version to snapshot meta. Also, `rpm-ostree kargs` with an update staged acts on the deployment that boots next and creates another one; a one-time GRUB edit avoids that.

The VDIMM proxy depends on DRAM Termination. Gigabyte exposes 'DRAM Termination (CH A/B)' (manual p.28 voltage list), so IT8792E in1 (DDRVTT AB) equals VDIMM/2 only while that setting is Auto. Both the '~1.53-1.56 V' estimate in the facts report and the proposed post-flash check assume Auto. Record the setting from the BIOS screens before relying on 2 x in1.

SVM is disabled ('svm' missing from /proc/cpuinfo, no /dev/kvm) while the user is in the 'libvirt' group (id output). Optimized Defaults keeps SVM Disabled (manual p.27).
